News.title: Female dance instructor, 23, charged with sexually abusing two teen students at her studio

Add us as a preferred source

TWISTED MISS Female dance instructor, 23, charged with sexually abusing two teen students at her studio

A DISGRACED dance teacher has been accused of sexually abusing two of her students – with cops alleging there may be several more victims.

Emily Pryor Albino, 23, taught children at X-Treme Dance Studio in Laurel, Delaware before being arrested after a chilling tip-off.



The Delaware studio offers classes to “all ages, from toddlers to adult fitness enthusiasts” according to its Facebook page.

A bombshell report to police on Tuesday alleged that Albino had sexually assaulted two of her teen dance pupils.



Detectives immediately launched a probe – and arrested Albino two days later.

She was charged with four counts of first-degree sexual abuse of a child.

Officers also said that the suspected sex pest had exchanged explicit messages with her students.

The exact age and gender of the alleged victims has not been made public.

It is also unclear who tipped off the police.

In a disturbing twist, detectives believe Albino may have abused other dance pupils who have not yet come forward.



The dance instructor was arrested on Thursday and jailed on a $110,000 bond, according to authorities.

If convicted, she could face life imprisonment.

The 23-year-old worked alongside her mother and sister at X-Treme Dance Studio, reported the Daily Mail.



The mum and sister have not been accused of any crimes.

The Sun has contacted X-Treme Dance Studio to find out which age groups Albino typically taught and whether she has been suspended pending investigations.

It comes after a science teacher, 25, was arrested after allegedly hooking up with a pupil in her car and in a closet on school property.

The twisted teacher taught Biology at Alexander High School in Douglasville in Georgia.

Maria Nichols is accused of having sex with a pupil in a cupboard between classrooms on April 23.

News.title: ‘Angel’ mum, 28, and her two dogs were killed by dangerous drivers as they used pedestrian crossing, court hears
News.content:
FAMILY HEARTBREAK ‘Angel’ mum, 28, and her two dogs were killed by dangerous drivers as they used pedestrian crossing, court hears

A MUM and her two dogs were killed by dangerous drivers while going over a pedestrian crossing, a court heard.

“Bubbly” Laura Sone-Demetrious was crossing a busy road on her evening dog walk when she was run over by a car that allegedly fled the scene.

The 28-year-old Arsenal fan, who worked in Tottenham Stadium, tragically died alongside her beloved pets on the A10 in Enfield, north London, in January 2024.

Cops identified her body by her dog’s name tag.





Sedor Olmez and Roderick Mirzakhanian are in court accused of causing her death by dangerous driving.

Olmez, 20, and Mirzakhanian, 31, both of Tottenham, north London, appeared at Highbury Corner Magistrates’ Court today.

Members of her family packed out the public gallery.

After Laura’s death, her devastated family paid tribute to the “angel in disguise”.



Her dad Peter wrote on Facebook: “This is the most unhappy day of my life, very early this morning I was awoken by a phone call from my youngest daughter to tell me, my oldest daughter has been run over and killed.

“I keep hoping she will call again and say she didn’t mean it.”

Her sister Gina said told the Independent at the time: “Laura was my oldest sister. She meant the world to me.

“Laura was an angel in disguise. She was a very bubbly, outgoing and caring young lady.



“She used to dance with or even without music.

“She danced with her dogs and even spoke to them as if they were human.

“She was loved by many, she was a family lady. It’s just very tragic how she passed.”

In 2017, Nilgün Akgün, 44, also died as she tried to cross the same junction on the A10.

Olmez wore a white shirt, patterned tie, and black jacket in the dock while Mirzakhanian wore a white shirt, and both spoke only to confirm their personal details in the short hearing.



They were not asked to enter pleas.

Olmez was also charged with driving a BMW that was uninsured in the incident on January 9.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The chairman of a bench of magistrates told the defendants: “Look, we can’t deal with this today, it’s called indictable only, it’s so serious that it’s beyond our sentencing powers if you were to be found guilty.”

Olmez and Mirzakhanian were freed on unconditional bail and told to attend the Old Bailey for a plea and trial preparation hearing on September 4.

News.title: Paedo Rolf Harris’ rotting riverside mansion is being ‘gutted’ by builders as new owners give creepy property makeover
News.content:
PAEDO Rolf Harris’s former riverside home is now being “gutted” by builders after it was finally flogged at auction last month.

The Sun can reveal the new owners have builders stripping the property that the pervert died in back in 2023 as part of a major makeover.



These exclusive pictures show a skip piled high outside the property while workmen tear out the interior of the notorious home.

One builder explained: “We are tearing all of the interior down so the new owners can make it their own.



“At this stage I am not sure what they plan to do with it, but we will get further instructions as and when.

“First thing’s first however is to strip everything back.”





The dilapidated four-bedroom property, on the banks of the River Thames in Bray, was listed in previous auctions with an asking price of £4million.

Though it later went to auction with a guide price of £1.95million but failed to meet its reserve after bidding stalled at £1.52million.

The asking price was repeatedly slashed before it finally changed hands under the hammer last month for around £1.6million.

Land Registry records show Deborah Developments International Limited is in the process of completing the purchase.

The company is run by Elaine Burke and Peter Titterell, whose catering business has worked on major films including James Bond blockbuster The World Is Not Enough.



The sale comes after Harris’s only daughter, Bindi, inherited the property along with the bulk of his £16million estate – documents also show there was no mortgage secured against the house.

The property was marketed as offering 6,440sq ft of living space, four bedrooms, numerous balconies overlooking the Thames and extensive riverside gardens.

The sale listing for the Bray home carried an unusual warning which read: “Prospective buyers are advised that there is a sensitive matter regarding this lot.”



One neighbour told The Sun the new owners are keen to give the house a fresh start.

“We all want to move on and put this awful stage behind us,” the woman, who did not want to be named, said.

“The man has been dead for several years now so I really hope now that the house has been sold we can finally move on.



“This is a lovely area to live, but Rolf committing his crimes here has really marred the area. We all want to move on.”

Unbelievably, one woman who lives nearby, when telling our reporter to leave, tried to claim her former neighbour Rolf had only slept with people “aged 18”.

Our reporter and photographer pointed out that people do not go to prison for having consensual sex with adults.

The woman then claimed she didn’t know Rolf “that well”, and when asked “how well” she knew the pervert, the neighbour declined to comment before marching off in a fluster.

Another local previously branded the original £4million asking price “cuckoo”, adding: “The sins happened in that house – it needs knocking down.”



In March 2013, Harris was one of 12 people arrested for questioning over historical allegations of sex offences as part of Operation Yewtree.



He was subsequently tried at Southwark Crown Court in 2014 on multiple counts of indecent assault against four female victims, aged between eight and 19.

After undergoing a lengthy trial, Harris was convicted of 11 counts of indecent assault and sentenced to five years in prison.

Following his conviction, he was stripped of his official honours including his CBE and Order of Australia and served nearly three years at HM Prison Stafford before his release on license in 2017.

He returned to living at the property and remained out of the public eye until his death in 2023.

A recent documentary, Rolf Harris: Primetime Predator, revealed the house was searched by police during Operation Yewtree in 2013.



It also claimed Harris was viewing indecent images of children there on the day of the late Queen’s Diamond Jubilee concert in 2012 before later appearing in a televised birthday tribute watched by millions.

Following Harris’s death from throat and neck cancer, Alwen died after suffering a stroke in 2024.

News.title: New school attendance rule is being rolled out across England next month in major crackdown
News.content:
A NEW school attendance rule will be rolled out across England next month, as the government looks to crackdown on pupil absence rates.

This comes as the number of children missing days of school remains above pre-pandemic levels.

Schools across England will now be given targets to improve pupil attendance rates.



The Department for Education (DfE) has confirmed that every state school in England will be given personalised pupil attendance targets, which would be monitored.



This comes in an effort to raise the number of pupils within education, as one in five pupils continue to miss at least 10 per cent of schooling.

According to official attendance data released yesterday (August 6), absence rates remain above pre-pandemic levels, with an overall attendance rate of 93 per cent for the 2025/26 academic year.

This is almost three per cent lower compared to the roughly 96 per cent attendance rate during the 2018/19 academic year.



As a result, education minister, Paul Waugh, told the BBC that the attendance targets would take each school’s local challenges into account, but “every school has a role to play to improve attendance”.

Schools have also been encouraged to offer more activities on Fridays, to improve attendance at the end of the week.

Although there would reportedly be no penalties for missed targets, the DfE will contact schools that are off-track to ensure they are taking action.

The school may then be encouraged join with other educational instituions in a local behaviour and attendance hub.



Since the start of the 2024/25 academic year, the government made it mandatory for schools to share their attendance records with the DfE.

In turn, Waugh has promised schools with better access to data tools to help them identify areas of concern quicker within individual pupils’ attendance records.

News.title: Russian ‘honeytraps’ luring Ukrainians to their deaths after tragic soldier who trained in UK drinks poison-laced booze
News.content:
A YOUNG Ukrainian soldier trained in the UK was allegedly poisoned in a twisted Russian honeytrap by a spy he fell in love with.

Mykyta Orlykivskyi, 23, was found dead inside his flat in a suspected suicide before doctors revealed he had consumed booze laced with deadly toxins.



Detectives working on Mykyta’s death quickly noticed several worrying signs which his grieving family now claim point to it being a Russian FSB-style attack.

Back in April, Mykyta told his loved ones he had met a woman after she reached out to him on Telegram claiming the pair had matched on a dating app.



Mykyta confessed to never using the apps but found her attractive so continued to speak to her after the pair exchanged photos.

His heartbroken aunt Tetiana Apalko, 53, told The Times that the mystery woman, aged 30, was only known as Rodnaya, meaning darling in Russian.



One of the first conversations the pair had was around Mykyta being a soldier, according to Tetiana.

Rodnaya had asked him to send her a photo of himself in his uniform which Mykyta replied with an image of him undergoing military training in the UK at the start of 2024.

Tetiana claims it was all a ploy to make sure her young nephew was working for Ukraine.

She said: “For the Russian security services it was proof that he was really a soldier. They didn’t need anything else.”



Rodnaya would then send him back AI-edited images of her smiling alongside the real picture of Mykyta.

The suspected spy, who said she was from Kharkiv, would spend the next two months growing close with Mykyta and even initiating video calls.

Mykyta loved the calls but noted the woman would always be sat on her own in front of a plain, white background, Tetiana said.



At the end of May, the young couple agreed to finally meet up in Zhytomyr where Mykyta was from.

On the day of the date, Rodnaya said she was having travel issues meaning she couldn’t come and would send him a present – said to be a bottle of whisky – to say sorry.

Shortly after the failed meet-up, Mykyta was found dead inside his home surrounded by the bottle of liquor and a Swiss army knife on June 9.

Detectives searched his flat and uncovered a string of messages and calls between the young Ukrainian and Rodnaya.

One of the phone calls happened at around the same time he started to drink the poisoned booze, Tetiana said.



Another call was made shortly after Mykyta was found with investigators probing if the call was designed to find out if he had drunk the drink yet.

Cops later traced the delivery of the whisky and found it hadn’t been sent from anyone resembling Rodnaya.

Detectives believe a 19-year-old man from Poltava, in central Ukraine, had also been recruited on Telegram to inject poison into the bottle and send it on to Mykyta.

Tetiana claims she was told the deal was made for the equivalent of a measly £80.

An investigation has also now revealed that cops are probing the theory the woman messaging Mykyta for several months was actually locked up in a Russian jail in Donetsk.



Part of the suspicions come from the white background she would always use when calling Mykyta.

Investigations are ongoing with cops yet to announce if they suspect any Russian influence.

An emotional Tetiana paid tribute to her nephew saying: “His whole life was ahead of him.

“It’s just so cynical. How is it possible that she could confess her love to him, while all the time knowing that she was going to murder him?”

If found to be a result of a Russian honeytrap then it would mark another deadly assault on Ukrainian soldiers by the Kremlin.



Back in January, a woman invited a soldier on a date in Zaporizhzhia but he was stabbed six times by a man in a balaclava in a coordinated attack.

In April, a 26-year-old woman from Zaporizhzhia was accused of stealing information from a soldier’s phone before poisoning him.

Investigators claim the woman was offered £2,800 from Russian spies to kill the Ukrainian man.

Another two teen girls are accused of poisoning a soldier with methadone in January.

The youngsters filmed the man as he died before allegedly sending it to their FSB handler.



There have also been several worrying cases of Ukrainian women catfishing Russian soldiers on dating apps and passing on the information to the Russians so they can pinpoint their locations.

News.title: Fugitive gang kingpin ‘Pablo Picasso’ who lived high life in Dubai while directing criminal drug network in UK is jailed
News.content:
'COCAINE ARTIST' Fugitive gang kingpin ‘Pablo Picasso’ who lived high life in Dubai while directing criminal drug network in UK is jailed

A FUGITIVE drug kingpin who called himself “Pablo Picasso” and boasted of being a “cocaine artist” as he directed a criminal drug network from overseas has been jailed.

Warren Barnes, 38, spent four-and-a-half years on the run living the high life in Dubai, Spain and Canada.



While residing abroad, Barnes pulled the strings of a drugs and money laundering gang as he evaded authorities.

He used “trusted associates” to oversee drug supply and move cash around the region, Greater Manchester Police said.



But the brazen crook has now been locked up for over 10 years alongside two associates following a sentencing hearing at Manchester Crown Court.

Barnes’ co-defendants, father and son duo Paul and Adam Taylor, have also been handed prison sentences for their roles in the syndicate.



The downfall of the criminal enterprise began in May 2023 when officers executed a warrant at Paul Taylor’s home.

Members of the Salford Challenger team targeted the property belonging to the 49-year-old.

Upon the arrival of the police, Taylor admitted that there were drugs inside the premises.

A search uncovered 182g of cocaine, more than 3kg of cannabis, and £5,000 in cash while officers also seized scales and snap bags from the property.



The illicit haul seized by the team had an estimated street value of over £45,000.

An examination of a mobile phone revealed Paul Taylor had used encrypted communication platforms – operating under the username Del Boy.

Detectives established he was in regular contact with Barnes, who used the handle “Pablo Picasso” and referred to himself as a “cocaine artist”.

Messages proved Barnes directed Paul Taylor to supply class A and B drugs, manage finances, and instructed him on how to run cannabis farms while he was out of the country.



Barnes was arrested in August last year after being stopped in Bolton, having spent four-and-a-half years on the run.

He had failed to answer bail in relation to a conspiracy to produce cannabis charge dating back to 2015.

Three mobile phones were seized from Barnes, two of which were encrypted.

It emerged he had spent time in Dubai, Spain and Canada while continuing to direct his illicit operation while images showing his swanky life on the run abroad were also recovered.



In total, Barnes is thought to have been responsible for “orchestrating the supply” of around 11kg of cocaine and about 159kg of cannabis.

Debtor lists and evidence of cryptocurrency transactions “used to launder criminal proceeds” were found by investigators.

Barnes, of no fixed address, was jailed for 10 years and six months.

He was convicted of two counts of being concerned in the supply of class A drugs (cocaine); two counts of being concerned in the supply of class B drugs (cannabis); one count of possession of a class A drug; one count of conspiring to produce a class B drug; one count of being concerned in the movement of money; and one count of possessing criminal property.

Paul Taylor had roped in his son Adam, who was involved in the cultivation and maintenance of cannabis plants, said cops.



Taylor, of Swinton, Salford, was jailed for five years three months.

He was convicted of one count of possession with intent to supply cocaine and cannabis; one count of being concerned in the supply of cocaine and cannabis; one count of being concerned in the production of cannabis; one count of being concerned in the movement of money; and one count of possessing criminal property.

Adam Taylor, of Peel Green Road, Eccles, Salford, was jailed for three years.

He was convicted of one count of being concerned in the supply of cocaine, cannabis and ketamine; one count of being concerned in the production of cannabis; and one count of possession with intent to supply cannabis.

Police Constable Brown, of GMP’s Serious and Organised Crime Group, said: “This investigation exposed an organised crime group that relied heavily on trusted associates to facilitate the large-scale supply of illegal drugs and the laundering of criminal profits.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Despite spending years outside the UK, Barnes continued to direct offending from abroad, believing distance and encrypted communications would protect him from law enforcement. He was wrong.

“The evidence gathered by investigators clearly demonstrated the scale of this operation and the roles played by those involved.”

News.title: Wife’s panic, mystery ‘old man’ & jawdropping confidence… Biggest bombshells in ‘suitcase killer’ case as Afghan charged
News.content:
THE biggest bombshells in the horrifying case of an Afghan boxer accused of murdering a Brit and stuffing her body in a suitcase have been revealed.

From the accused killer’s horrified wife connecting the dots to an alibi involving a mystery old man, shocking revelations continue to rock the Athens courthouse where Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, has been charged with murder.



The Afghan was formally charged with intentional homicide, robbery and illegal possession of a weapon yesterday, nearly three weeks after Elisabeth Ross’ body was found stuffed in a suitcase.

Ahmadzai has already admitted to putting her body into the suitcase and taking her to the abandoned site where she was found.



But he has continued to deny murdering Elisabeth.

Panicked wife’s ‘key’ evidence

The “cunning” Afghan boxer was snared after his terrified wife raised suspicions about his alibi and provided testimony to the police.



On July 15, Ahmadzai’s American wife Alaina says she saw a text message sent from Elisabeth to him which read: “Thank you for your intention to come with me.”

Later that night, Alaina claimed in her testimony that she woke up and found her husband had left their home without any warning.

She said: “I checked his location on my cell phone. I saw that he was inside the apartment on Rethymno Street.

“I was surprised because there was no particular reason for him to be there at that time.”



She phoned him up and he said he was out watching a football match at a cafe and had headed inside the apartment to just use the toilet.

At the time, Alaina said she believed his football story as one of his family members had died on the same day.

But over the next fortnight, she noticed odd behaviour from her husband.



He bought her a flashy new phone and allegedly attempted to give his wife €2,550 (£2,200) in cash.

Alaina later turned these items over to the police, suspecting that they were bought using stolen funds from the victim.

On July 18, news broke that a woman had been found dead inside a suitcase close to where the couple lived.

The victim’s identity was yet to be revealed but Alaina says she woke up in the middle of the night on July 29 and thought it could be Elisabeth.

The pair hadn’t spoken for weeks now so Alaina quickly messaged the Brit and received two concerning replies.



Alaina said: “These messages were not in Lisa’s style both in terms of her level of English and the use of emojis that she never used.”

After failing to reach her on a call, Alaina said she started to think about the possibility that Elisabeth could be the woman in the suitcase.

She later told police: “All of the above made me feel strange. Especially combining the dates, the messages and my husband’s behavior.



“I have various thoughts that make me feel uncomfortable.”

After the body was identified as Elisabeth, the wife said she became so afraid that she and her husband left their home and spent the night in different places.

The mystery ‘old man’

After his arrest, Ahmadzai claimed that he found Elisabeth dead at her rental apartment and tried to flee the scene.

But in a bizarre twist, he told the court that he bumped into an old man who advised him to dump the remains in an abandoned building nearby.

The mystery new character was not mentioned in his initial interview with police.



Ahmadzai said he returned to the apartment the next day, placed Elisabeth’s body in a suitcase and drove it through Athens.

He told cops: “He told me to leave the suitcase with him and he would take care of it.”

The Afghan then confessed to withdrawing €10,000 (£8,500) from ATMs in Greece using stolen credit cards that belonged to the victim.

Accused killer’s shocking confidence

As he continued to deny murdering Elisabeth, Ahmadzai was said to be “confident to the point of disbelief” during his second court hearing.

The courthouse is located on Evelpidon Street in the Greek capital – just a few minutes away from where Elisabeth’s body was found.



The alleged killer covered part of his face with his jumper as he was hauled into the session by armed and masked officers.

His lawyer Christos Erdas confirmed Ahmadzai did not speak during the hearing or submit a plea for any of the three charges he faces.

He is yet to have any visits behind bars, including from his wife and mother to his child Alaina, a well-placed source told the Sun.

Erdas tried to delay the murder probe, but magistrates handling the case unanimously agreed he should be charged on intentional homicide, robbery and illegal possession of a weapon.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Police sources say they are “100 per cent” certain Ahmadzai is involved in her death after he confessed to hiding her body in a suitcase last week.



But investigators are still looking for potential accomplices, The Sun has learned.

News.title: Two more arrests in third night of disorder in Thetford as protesters lob eggs at migrant homes & cops escort them away
News.content:
COPS have arrested two more people amid chaotic protests that saw eggs lobbed at homes believed to be housing migrants.

Asylum seekers had to be escorted away from properties in Thetford, Norfolk, following the third successive night of unrest in the area.



Some forty Norfolk Police officers descended on the market town last night after a mob had previously tried to force their way into homes.

Cops had been granted a dispersal order after a female police officer was bitten the previous night.



The crowd, believed to be up to 100 people, were seen shouting and attempting to gain access to the homes in St John’s Way on Wednesday.

Two men in their 40s have since been arrested, bringing the total number held over the protests to five, the force confirmed.

One was arrested on suspicion of inciting racial hatred.

The other was held on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly and failing to provide details to police when asked.



And Norfolk County Councillor Scott Hussey claimed cops were yesterday dispersing crowds for “lobbing eggs” at migrant homes.

He posted videos on Facebook showing officers piling out of police vans and marching towards crowds of people in the area.

Norfolk Police’s Chief Constable Paul Sanford said asylum seekers had to be escorted from homes following the chaos.

He told the BBC’s Today programme: “We did have people protesting who were targeting addresses they believed were housing asylum seekers.

“On a couple of occasions, that required us to escort the residents of those properties away for their safety.”



“I think it’s highly likely that the protesters would have got into the property.

“They would have created a significant problem, and really threatened the safety of the occupants, and indeed the protesters themselves.”

Police said dozens of protesters had attempted to force entry to a home by smashing a window, fence panel and letterbox on Wednesday.



Two officers were rushed to hospital after responding to the scene after one was hit by a rock, one bitten and another spat at.

Police described the protests as “fast-moving and volatile”, with tensions escalating as a crowd moved towards a residential property.

Last night, six officers remained outside the three-storey property on Chester Way.

Pictures showed cops speaking with residents, wearing high-viz jackets but with riot helmets on their hips.

Mr Sanford went on to defend his officer’s actions and warned those involved in the protests would face the “full force of the law“.



He added: “There are people living in Thetford who are understandably concerned about some of the things that are happening in their town.

“However, across three consecutive nights, a group of people have crossed the line as to what is acceptable.

“And we have been appropriately policing those behaviours. I’ve seen the reports of heavy handedness.

“We’ve been firm… we’ve been firm with people who have broken the law.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I’ve had two police officers hospitalised as a result of the incident on Wednesday night.



“The people who perpetrated those offences should expect the full force of the law, and I will be pushing for the strongest possible sanction.”

News.title: Europe-wide terror concern amid rise of ISIS-inspired attacks and radicalisation
News.content:
Europe-wide terror concern amid rise of ISIS-inspired attacks and radicalisation

World most terrifying terror group ISIS - "self-dubbed 'al-Qaeda on steroids" is on the rise again across Europe, sparking fears it has found innovative ways of radicalising young exremists

View 4 Images Slain British ISIS terrorist Mohammed Emwazi - AKA JIhadi John (Image: Internet Unknown)

A growing number of thwarted and executed Islamic State-sponsored terror attacks across Europe have sparked fears terrorism is once again on the rise across the continent, according to a new report.

‌



The most feared terror network the world has ever known is growing again, and individuals and groups are being radicalised at a terrifying rate, according to sources. Terror threats across Europe, including the UK, could spark a reaction from far-right extremism, prompting a self-perpetuating competition between militant Islamists and anti-Islam groups.

‌



There is also alarm over growing links between terror groups such as ISIS, al-Qaeda and shadowy groups loyal to Iran, such as Hezbollah-affiliates in Lebanon and Syria.

‌



A European security source told the Mirror: "The rise of ISIS-inspired attacks across Europe is a cause of huge concern. History shows that they do trigger further attacks by inspiring others, this is then producing a cycle of increasing right wing political responses and right wing groups gaining traction and vigilante type attacks. There is huge concern in the EU community."

Masked gunmen warn tourists to stay away from popular holiday hotspot READ MORE :

View 4 Images Alexanda Kotey, from London, said 'we were al-Qaeda on steroids' (Image: Rowan Griffiths \\ Daily Mirror)

Terror plots 'shine light on evolving terrorism landscape'

Respected former FBI terror expert Ali Soufan’s organisation, The Soufan Centre, highlighted the alarm over ISIS in Europe, including in the UK, in the recent report.

‌



It highlights fears ISIS and other foreign terror groups have stepped up a campaign, twisting the minds of mostly young men of what it describes "indirect influence through online radicalisation and engagement."

This means ISIS operatives may have found a more subtle and persuasive method of appealing to vulnerable would-be terrorists than direct invitations to join their terror campaign. And subtle radicalisation means the group is increasingly at arms-length contact with European extremists online but in ways that are far less traceable than those previously used.

Now the Soufan Centre, a US-based non-profit organisation warned: "A string of thwarted and executed attacks across Europe — many either proven or suspected to be aligned with the Islamic State (IS) — have shined a light on an evolving terrorism landscape.

‌



"Recent attack plots and terrorism charges in Europe have featured youth suspects, highlighting a concerning risk matrix of online radicalization and coordination with foreign terrorist networks, creating challenges for law enforcement agencies. Recent cases have not revealed embedded foreign terrorist networks in European cities, but rather indirect influence through online radicalization and engagement, demonstrating a more passive dynamic that make detection, prevention, and interdiction difficult."

View 4 Images Mirror's Chris Hughes interviews Kotey in jail (Image: Rowan Griffiths \\ Daily Mirror)

Alexanda Kotey's smirk during Mirror interview

A huge military campaign led by Iraqi and Syrian Kurds, supported by US special forces, effectively demolished ISIS’s ability to hold ground in the Middle East by 2019. In particular, members of British Islamic State groups in Syria, led by Mohammed Emwazi-AKA ‘Jhadi John,’ were killed or arrested by Syrian Kurds.

‌



Emwazi was killed by a Hellfire missile attack in 2015 and Alexanda Kotey and El Shafee Elsheikh are thought to be behind bars in a US Supermax prison in Colorado. But since then, US withdrawals from Syria and partial down-sizing of its military in Iraq have led to a resurgence of the group, even in Africa and elsewhere across Asia.

Evil Kotey laughed when he told the Daily Mirror, during an interview conducted in his jail in Syria in 2019: "Joining Islamic State was like being in al-Qaeda on steroids." But the future he feared more than anything was being caught and jailed in the US, which is exactly what happened.

View 4 Images The Iran war has triggered terror fears as US clamps down on Strait of Hormuz (Image: US Central Command (CENTCOM)/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Huge concern about radicalisation

Taliban rule in Afghanistan since the chaotic and disastrous withdrawal in 2021 also prompted ISIS to grow in the region, in Pakistan and even in India in the form of ISIS in the Khorasan.

Now European agencies are under pressure for not having been able to disrupt or tackle terror plots in countries such as France and Germany The Soufan report adds: “...plots, arrests and attacks have drawn in criticism across the political spectrum in France and Germany where there were recent deadly attacks that highlight lapses prevention, deradicalisation and post-attack investigation processes.”

In the UK there has been alarm over a huge increase in reporting of young victims of radicalisation to the government anti-terror Prevent scheme.

Article continues below

Last month, Italian authorities arrested a teenage girl in Pavia on terror charges after she was suspected of being involved in ISIS related social media. She was suspected of participating in pro-ISIS Telegram conversations and downloading bomb-making instructions. On July 25, French police raided a six member cell of terror suspects over a plot to attack a Jewish synagogue in Sarcelles, outside Paris. Other plots, according to the Soufan Centre “against Jewish community sites have been flagged elsewhere in Europe and North America particularly since the outbreak of the Iran war.”

These plots are often linked to Iran backed militia such as Kataib Hezbollah or crime gangs with Iranian links. On the same day as the foiled plot in Sarcelles a Berlin Pride event was attacked by a German of Lebanese descent called Abdul Ballout. Ballout, an ISIS loyalist killed one and injured 31 others in a car-ramming and stabbing spree. On July 27 another individual armed with knives stabbed three women in Paris.

News.title: Mastercard compensation update as £100million put aside to repay UK shoppers
News.content:
Mastercard compensation update as £100million put aside to repay UK shoppers

Walter Merricks, a former financial ombudsman, argued that 46 million shoppers were ripped off after fees were wrongly levied on transactions between 1992 and 2008

View 2 Images Mastercard has agreed to settle the claim (Image: LightRocket via Getty Images)

Millions of shoppers who are awaiting compensation following a landmark case against Mastercard have been given an update this week.

‌



Walter Merricks, a former financial ombudsman, argued that 46 million shoppers were ripped off after fees were wrongly levied on transactions between 1992 and 2008. The fees were paid by retailers accepting Mastercard payments, rather than by customers themselves - meaning you don't necessarily need to have owned a Mastercard to be eligible for compensation.

‌



It is estimated that around 2.3 million people are expected to come forward to claim, with £100million ringfenced for consumers. If this happens, each person would get £45. If fewer people than expected claim, the maximum each person will get is £70.

‌



View 2 Images You could be due up to £70 depending on how many people claim

However, consumers have not been able to submit their details yet, as the online claims portal was delayed following a legal challenge. But in an update this week, Mr Merricks announced that the legal claims have now been dropped, and anyone affected will be able to start the process of starting to claim compensation by the end of this year.

‌



He said: "This finally opens the way for me to prepare for distribution of at least £100m to consumers. This is presently the largest amount ever secured from group litigation for the benefit of UK consumers."

Mr Merricks added: "When we are ready to launch (which will be in the coming months) there will be a nation-wide publicity campaign to alert people and a 6-month period during which people will be able to register their claim. The £100m will be divided equally between the people who claim, and the expectation is that consumers should get a minimum of £45, which could rise to as much as £70 depending on the numbers that claim. So for a couple this could be between £90 and £140."

News.title: Royal Mail worker explains why post is folded before putting it in letterboxes
News.content:
Royal Mail worker explains why post is folded before putting it in letterboxes

A Royal Mail employee explained the reason why postmen and postwomen sometimes fold letters before they put them through letterboxes - and it is a surprisingly simple justification

View 3 Images A Royal Mail worker once explained why they fold letters before posting them (stock) (Image: Getty)

A Royal Mail worker explained why post is folded before it is put through letterboxes, and the reason is surprisingly simple.

‌



Appearing on an episode of Things People Do, the anonymous postal worker explained to former professional rugby player Joe Marler why post is folded before it is put through a letterbox.

‌



The Royal Mail employee, who was given a pseudonym for the purposes of the interview, said the reason why it was sometimes folded was simply because it was easier to get it through the slot.

‌



He said: “I favour the old fold before I post because I find it easier to get through a letterbox. So, when you’re doing that you can normally feel what’s in there…I try to get that all in one go. It’s easier to get through the letterbox.”

However, he admitted that he doesn’t fold every letter, especially if it’s a special greetings card or something being sent to mark someone’s birthday. They added: “I don’t fold people’s cards, birthday cards I don’t do that.”

View 3 Images The Royal Mail has given guidance on how to post letters too (stock) (Image: Getty)

‌



It is not known whether this postal worker still works for the postal service, but more recently the Royal Mail has issued some critical advice to people who write addresses on envelops in pen ink.

They emphasised how important it is for people to make sure the address they put on their envelope, if they are going to write it by hand, is legible to ensure it reaches its intended destination.

The reason for this is so the Royal Mail’s reading and sorting machines can better understand it and send the letter or parcel on its way.

‌



In the guidance, posted on the postal services’ website, they said: “Use clear and easy to read handwriting (or font if you are printing the address).

“Use a pen or ink that is clear against the colour of the envelope or parcel. It's important that the address shows up against the colour of your envelope… Write the address clearly on the front, following our guidelines, and always include a postcode if possible."

View 3 Images The Royal Mail has faced issues in recent days (stock) (Image: Getty)

‌



The Royal Mail’s guidance comes at a time when they have admitted some people may be facing some delays to their post if they live in one of 127 postcodes.

The problems, they said, were being found in “a small number of local offices” which they said were due to a variety of issues.

In a statement, they, before going onto apologise for the issues, said: “This may temporarily not be possible due to local issues such as high levels of sick absence, resourcing, or other local factors. In those cases, we will rotate deliveries to minimise the delay to individual customers.

Article continues below

“We also provide targeted support to those offices to address their challenges and restore our service to the high standard our customers would normally receive.”

News.content:
A lorry is on fire on the M6

M6 traffic live: Motorway closed in West Midlands with lorry on fire

News.title: Solar eclipse 2026 maps reveal best places in UK to watch stunning show
News.content:
Solar eclipse 2026 maps reveal best places in UK to watch stunning show

The most significant solar eclipse since 1999 is just days away and will be visible from the UK - but people in some areas will have a better view than others

View 3 Images The Moon will appear to take a 'bite' out of the Sun (stock) (Image: Getty)

The UK is just a few days away from a much awaited solar eclipse - the most significant since 1999.

‌



On Wednesday next week, the Moon will pass directly between the Earth and the Sun, blocking the Sun's face and leaving a narrow strip of the Earth's surface in darkness. The European Space Agency states: "With the Sun’s dazzling disc covered, we get a unique chance to see its wispy atmosphere.

‌



"Stars and planets appear in the sky. The temperature drops. The wind picks up. And birds and insects may behave as if it’s nighttime."

‌



The solar eclipse will be visible across much of Europe and will even reach full totality in some places including Spain, Portugal and Iceland. This won't be the case in the UK on this occasion, however, many places around the country will be able to observe up to 96 per cent coverage.

View 3 Images Exeter is one of the cities where greatest coverage will be observed

Where to see total solar eclipse 2026 as Brit holiday hotspots set for stunning show READ MORE :

This means the Moon will appear to take a "bite" out of the Sun, dimming its light slightly and leading to twilight conditions. The last total eclipse visible from the UK was on August 11, 1999, with Cornwall and parts of Devon in the path of totality.

‌



Cornwall and Devon will also be the region where this month's eclipse will see most of the Sun covered. Penzance, for example, will get 95.76 per cent, reached at 7.16pm.

Hugh Town in the Isles of Scilly will reach 96.44 per cent, with most of the UK coverage being above 90 per cent, making it the deepest solar eclipse here since 1999.

News.title: 'Make shower switch' to slash energy bills this summer
News.content:
'Make shower switch' to slash energy bills this summer

Ofgem has shared a energy-saving tips for Brits to take advantage of

View 2 Images Simple behavioural changes featured heavily in Ofgem advice (Image: Emilija Manevska via Getty Images)

Households have been given a ten-point plan issued by the energy regulator to help slash sky-high bills.

‌



Ofgem, the industry watchdog, took to social media to set out a checklist of simple changes that families can make around the house - insisting that even small tweaks to daily habits can deliver significant savings. Chief among the tips is the advice to swap baths for showers, with the regulator pointing out that heating a full tub of water uses considerably more energy than a quick wash under the shower head.

‌



But the bath-versus-shower switch was just one of ten money-saving measures set out by the watchdog in a post shared with its followers, under the heading: "Here are 10 energy saving tips that you can do around your house to reduce your energy usage and in turn reduce your energy bills."

‌



View 2 Images Families were also told to avoid using the tumble dryer where possible (Image: Mariyariya via Getty Images)

The regulator, which sets the notorious price cap reviewed every three months, was at pains to stress that the cap itself is only half the story - insisting that how much gas and electricity a household actually burns through has just as much bearing on the final bill.

Top of the list was insulation, with Ofgem urging homeowners to install or top up loft insulation to stop precious heat escaping through the roof - traditionally one of the biggest culprits for warmth leaking out of British homes.

‌



Families were also told to avoid using the tumble dryer where possible, with the appliance long known as one of the most power-hungry machines in the average home, guzzling electricity that can otherwise be saved by air-drying clothes.

Draught-proofing was another key recommendation, with the regulator advising households to seal gaps around doors and windows to keep the heat in - though it cautioned homeowners not to block ventilation channels in the process.

Simple behavioural changes featured heavily too. Ofgem said switching appliances off at the plug, rather than leaving them lurking on standby, could help chip away at bills, as could the age-old habit of turning off lights in empty rooms.

‌



Even laundry habits came under scrutiny, with the watchdog recommending a 30°C wash, a full drum and shorter cycles wherever possible - all of which, it said, reduce the energy needed to get clothes clean. Bulbs also made the cut, with households told that switching to energy-efficient LED lighting could save up to £4 per bulb every year - a modest saving on paper, but one that mounts up in a home with a dozen or more fittings.

Rounding off the list, Ofgem suggested fitting window film or secondary glazing, particularly in homes with older single-glazed windows, and insulating hot water tanks with lagging to cut the amount of heat lost from the cylinder.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



The advice lands as households continue to grapple with the lingering effects of the cost-of-living crisis, with millions still watching every penny as winter approaches.

Campaigners have long argued that while political rows over the price cap dominate headlines, it is often these unglamorous, practical steps - insulating, unplugging, washing at lower temperatures - that make the real difference to the final figure landing on the doormat.

News.title: Schoolgirl, 11, found dead after major search at Scotland beauty spot
News.content:
Schoolgirl, 11, found dead after major search at Scotland beauty spot

Police were called to the Gore Glen area near Gorebrige, with the incident taking place near a woodland park in Midlothian

View Image Police were called to the Gore Glen area yesterday

The body of an 11-year-old girl has been recovered from water near a woodland park in Scotland.

‌



Police were called to the Gore Glen area near Gorebridge in Midlothian around midday yesterday following concerns for the girl.

‌



The girl was found in the Gore Water near Shanks Bridge later in the afternoon and was pronounced dead at the scene.

‌



The death is now being treated as unexplained by officers and an investigation is ongoing.

A Police Scotland spokesperson told the Daily Record: "We were made aware of concern for an 11-year-old girl in the Gore Glen area, near Gorebridge around 12.40pm on Thursday, 6 August, 2026.

‌



"The body of the girl was found in the Gore Water near to Shanks Bridge around 4.25pm.

"She was pronounced dead at the scene and her family are aware.

"Her death is being treated as unexplained and enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

News.title: Man Utd legend's blazing row with staff at local tip – 'I'm banned now'
News.content:
Man Utd legend's blazing row with staff at local tip – 'I'm banned now'

Former Manchester United midfielder Nicky Butt was left fuming when he was stopped from entering his local tip in his Range Rover

Nicky Butt has been kicked out of his local tip after a 'raging row' with workers. Butt, one of the Class of 92, blew his top when staff branded his Range Rover a commercial vehicle because the seats were folded flat. He dumped his 'smelling bags' anyway, prompting an employee to sprint after him.

‌



According to The Sun, Butt said: "There's this guy at the gate bit, and he flags me down and goes, 'Put your windows down I need to look in the back of your car'. I'm going, 'What for?'

‌



"I've got a lot of crap from the house, bit of cardboard... I missed the bin man last week, so I've got a few smelly bags.

News.title: I was standing in front of my teacher when she was shot, Thai pupil says
News.content:
On Friday morning, as the final classes of the week were under way, panicked students began streaming out of a prestigious school just outside Bangkok.

Inside, police say, a 14-year-old boy had opened fire.

"I was standing in front of the teacher when she was shot," a shaken seventh grader tells the BBC, near the gates of Debsirin School in Nonthaburi. "She was talking to me when [the gunman] showed up."

Still in her uniform, with her mother by her side, she explains how the shooter stalked from room to room.

Authorities say he killed five teachers and injured more than 30 people - including fellow pupils - before turning the weapon on himself. Earlier, he had gunned down his grandparents.

"I had to climb over the school fence to escape with other friends," the girl, who the BBC is not naming, continues.

Her mother says the girl thought she might die. "[She said] 'I thought I'd never see you again'."

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, he said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: England footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub
News.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.

The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.

He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

News.title: Arrests in Norfolk town as disorder continues for third night
News.content:
The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, said the unrest had "put Thetford back decades" after years of trying to improve the town's reputation.

Speaking to the BBC on Friday, he said: "It's been awful the last few nights, it's been terrifying for many Thetford residents."

He said he had been made aware of properties being "pelted with eggs" on Thursday and said the town was "on edge".

He said the violence was "scaring and terrifying people who live in Thetford, particularly people from minority ethnic communities who are contacting me terrified that they are going to be misidentified as an asylum seeker and attacked".

He urged fellow politicians to "call out" the violent protests and assaults of police officers.

Jermy has previously called on the Home Office to end "secrecy and confusion" around plans to house more asylum seekers in former military barracks â including at RAF Barnham, near Thetford.

The town's mayor, Vic Peters, said he supported peaceful protests but condemned "willful disregard of the law".

He said in the past week council staff had been subjected to abuse and intimidation, including councillors, who have been verbally abused at and away from official council meetings.

He said he was commenting as an individual and not as an official statement by the town council.

Scott Hussey, a Reform councillor for the nearby Brecks division on Norfolk County Council, said a "peaceful protest" had started at the town's police station on Wednesday night before it moved to Clover Way.

He described the protest as "spirited" and said there had been "some skirmishes" but said he saw no violence.

He accused the Home Office of "opening a number of these HMOs across Thetford" and "trying to rush through the site for asylum seekers at Barnham".

A Home Office spokesperson condemned the behaviour, warning that "anyone taking part in this criminal activity will face the full force of the law".

They acknowledged concerns about immigration in Thetford but condemned the violence of some protesters.

A spokesperson said: "The right to protest is fundamental to our democracy and the concerns of communities are central to our immigration reforms."

News.title: How a diary entry solved the murder of a missing man
News.content:
When Det Con Tom Ryan came across a diary entry about an old cattle trailer in July 2025, he knew he had finally solved the murder of a man who had disappeared six years earlier.

Richard Dyson vanished without trace in November 2019. He was last seen alive on 17 November that year and was reported missing eight days later when he failed to meet his daughter, Bethany.

"He was by all accounts a very good father, and he was regularly in contact with his daughter Bethany who was, I believe, 19 at the time of his disappearance. It was totally out of character," Ryan recalled.

"It was clear that he had disappeared off the face of the Earth."

Richard, who was 55 at the time, had been living in his car at Parkside Cottage on Christopher Wright's farm on Sheffield Road in Barnsley, helping with small jobs around the farm.

The farm was searched, but other than a collection of illegal weapons belonging to Wright, nothing more unusual was found and there was no sign of Richard.

His phone, however, showed it had never left the farm.

Police believed from the outset that Richard had been killed and that Wright and his childhood friend, Karl Schwalbe, were responsible, according to Ryan.

"We very much suspected their involvement, but without a body it's very difficult to prove murder," he said.

On 28 July, Wright, 73, and Schwalbe, 72, were convicted for their roles in Richard's disappearance and murder, ending a six-year wait for answers for Richard's family.

At a sentencing hearing at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday, Wright was jailed for 35 years for murder and Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.

But how did police finally catch them?

News.title: Norway call for Infantino to resign as Mexico and Argentina back president
News.content:
Norway have called on Fifa president Gianni Infantino to resign following his aborted attempt to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, but Mexico and Argentina have voiced their support for the 56-year-old.

Norway have gone a step further than the football associations of England, Wales, Croatia and Albania, all of whom have withdrawn support for Infantino without explicitly calling for him to resign.

"He [Infantino] does not have the institutional trust required to govern Fifa stably in the times we are in," Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness said on Friday.

"There is no going back for Gianni Infantino. The international football cooperation is very much in trouble, and we must have a reason to get together now, and we want to ask the Fifa president to resign now.

"We will see which other countries eventually join in, if that becomes the strategy from the Uefa board. We are not going to ask for an extraordinary [Uefa board] meeting, we will ask him to resign in our dialogue with Fifa."

Klaveness, who is a qualified lawyer, went through a list of concerns that the Norwegian FA has expressed to Fifa during her four-year tenure.

Among them were questions around the awarding of tournaments, the inaugural Fifa peace prize that was awarded to US President âDonald Trump in December, and the overturning of a ban for American forward Folarin Balogun during the recent World Cup following a phone call from Trump.

Meanwhile, earlier on Friday the Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.

Concacaf, which runs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, called for a "comprehensive reckoning" of Infantino's presidency after he aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

However, 2026 World Cup co-hosts Mexico have backed Infantino's leadership amid widespread calls for him to resign.

"The FMF [Mexican FA] supports president Infantino's leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening," a statement read.

It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa members.

"The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework, and it joins the call made by president Infantino to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of the 211 member associations," it added.

News.title: Divers find 162-year-old Guinness in shipwreck off the English coast
News.content:
How far would you travel for a pint of Guinness? If the answer is to the bottom of the sea, you might be in luck.

There's just one catch - the pint in question is 162 years old.

When Belgian underwater photographer Stefan Panis discovered a bottle buried in a shipwreck off the coast of Dover in 2025, he had no idea what he had found. He just knew something about it had caught his eye.

When Panis and his friend, Eddie Huzzey, surfaced, a quick rinse revealed the familiar Guinness branding. The bottle dates back to 1864.

"We lifted the artefact, and then on the surface a quick rinse revealed 'Guinness'," he said.

News.title: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?
News.content:
Do you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?

The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more than 50 years and is still used by around half of all UK households.

But it has struggled to thrive in recent years amid fierce competition from online giants like Amazon, with sales stagnating.

Its owner Sainsbury's recently announced it was selling the chain for a lot less than it paid for it just 10 years ago.

But the new owners say they see "real opportunities" for growth, including opening new standalone shops. Can they succeed where Sainsbury's did not?

News.title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
News.content:
The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.

The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.

The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.

But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".

In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.

Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.

Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.

Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.

Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.

For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.

Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.

Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.

Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.

When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing.

There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people.

In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.

In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals.

The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.

News.title: NHS Tayside investigates data breach into Minnie Merriman medical records
News.content:
NHS Tayside is investigating an alleged data breach into the medical records of a nine-year-old girl at the centre of a murder probe in Arbroath.

Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, died at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee after being found seriously injured at an industrial estate in the town.

A 35-year-old man, who was known to the girl, has appeared in court charged with her murder.

NHS Tayside said it was "investigating the circumstances" of the alleged breach that happened in a clinical area where staff access patient information.

A spokesperson added : "As a matter of governance, any data protection breach would be recorded and investigated by NHS Tayside and, where appropriate, reported to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).

"It would not be appropriate for us to comment further on individual staffing matters."

News.title: Sullivan set to attend West Ham tie against advice
News.content:
West Ham are expecting David Sullivan to attend Saturday's Carabao Cup first-round tie against Portsmouth despite him being advised to stay away from home matches at London Stadium.

Sullivan, 77, resigned from his position as co-chair of West Ham in June after a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times revealed that seven women have accused Sullivan of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour.

He has categorically denied the allegations.

On Monday, a spokesperson for London Stadium told BBC News it had "recommended" to West Ham that Sullivan does not attend matches because of concerns about fan unrest.

London Stadium has asked for advance notice of any planned visits by major shareholder Sullivan - who retains a 38.8% stake in the club - in order to implement additional safety and operational measures.

The match against Portsmouth will be the first the club has played since the allegations against Sullivan were first reported.

The Panorama and Times joint investigation also revealed that Sullivan has been banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams for the past three years because of safeguarding concerns.

London Stadium was unaware of the restrictions until the BBC's report.

Sullivan was banned after a historical allegation about his conduct was raised with the Football Association in 2023. He has previously said the allegation was false.

Sullivan had already been the subject of intense fan abuse for his running of the club, who were relegated to the Championship last season for the first time since 2011.

Although West Ham have stabilised on the pitch, with key figures, including manager Nuno Espirito Santo and skipper Jarrod Bowen committing their future to the club, there remains huge uncertainty off it.

Vanessa Gold, daughter of Sullivan's late business partner and former West Ham co-chair David, backed out of a deal to sell part of her stake in the club to Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky, and instead reached an agreement with Amanda Staveley, the public face of the Saudi Arabia-backed takeover at Newcastle, to sell her entire 25.1% stake.

However, Kretinsky has since sold a small part of his own stake, bringing him under 25%.

That would allow him to buy Gold's shares under West Ham's pre-emption rights rules - which allow existing shareholders first choice to buy shares when they become available.

If he did so he would become West Ham's biggest shareholder, without triggering another clause that would force him to then buy the rest of the club.

It is anticipated Saturday's match against fellow Championship side Portsmouth (15:00 BST) will set an attendance record for an EFL Cup first-round tie, with the Hammers having sold 55,000 season tickets for the new campaign.

News.title: Girl, 11, found dead after major search launched at beauty spot
News.content:
An 11-year-old girl has died after being found in the water at a beauty spot in Midlothian.

A major search operation was launched after concerns were raised for a young girl in Gore Glen Woodland Park near Gorebridge at about 12:40 on Thursday.

The girl's body was found in the park's Gore Water, near Shank Bridge, at about 16:25. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A force spokesperson said: "Her death is being treated as unexplained and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

Police said her family were aware.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said it sent two appliances to the incident shortly before 16:30 to support emergency services partners.

News.title: Man 'humiliated' after being told mobility scooter too big for train
News.content:
A man with osteoarthritis and learning difficulties has said he feels "humiliated" after being told he cannot take his new mobility scooter on Translink's train services because it has been deemed to be too big.

Stephen Magee had been using his previous scooter for about five years without any problems.

But he said after Translink assessed his new scooter he was told it is 10cm too large.

A Translink spokesperson said the company was committed to providing accessible services for everyone and that all mobility scooters were assessed through an independent process to make sure they could be accommodated and taken on and off its vehicles safely.

Magee, who lives in Coleraine, said he bought the new scooter as the previous one had begun to show its age.

He originally contacted the Nolan Show to share his story.

He said he deliberately bought a scooter that was the same size as his old one, thinking it would be suitable to take onto trains, but after it was assessed he got a letter from Translink saying it was too big.

"I felt disheartened, I felt humiliated in so many ways," he said.

"I'm left not being able to go on any trains and I can't use the buses because it will not fit on any of their buses.

"It seems like we're [mobility scooter users] an inconvenience to people.

"I don't like the fact that I use a mobility scooter but unfortunately I've been left with no choice."

News.title: Police to end review into siblings who died in farmhouse 'bloodbath'
News.content:
A forensic review into the deaths of a brother and sister 50 years ago will end almost four years after it began, despite not delivering any new conclusions.

The bodies of Martha and Griff Thomas were found at a farmhouse in Llangolman, Pembrokeshire in 1976, originally prompting a double murder investigation.

Family member Huw Gibby, 79, said he was left "shell-shocked" that the investigation had failed to find any new answers, and described crime scene photos as a "bloodbath".

Dyfed-Powys Police said a "significant amount of complex work" had been undertaken, and "the family has been updated on the limitations faced in reviewing an incident that took place 50 years ago".

On a chilly Saturday morning in December 1976, postman Nigel Rossiter pulled up outside the isolated Ffynon Samson farmhouse in west Wales.

It was his first week in the job, and he spotted a couple of letters still lying on the floor of the porch where he had delivered them days before.

Smelling burning inside, he raised the alarm. This led to the discovery of two bodies â Griff, 73, who was badly burnt, and Martha, 70, who had severe injuries.

Police were called and found Martha - known as Patti - lying slumped on a magazine rack in the corner of the living room, with severe head injuries.

Chairs had been knocked over, and an overturned television lay at her feet. It was still switched on, with the sound of static filling the room.

News.title: Wildfire damage could take hundreds of years to recover from, experts say
News.content:
It could be hundreds of years before habitats destroyed by wildfires in Wales recover, an environment watchdog has said.

Nick Thomas, from Natural Resources Wales (NRW), said if soil had been incinerated in upland areas rich in peat, which grows at about a millimetre a year, it could take centuries for the vegetation to come back.

He expects 2026 to be the worst year Wales has ever experienced.

As well as damage to natural habitats and animal life, Thomas warned loss of soil could increase flood risks, because it no longer acted as a "sponge" holding water on high ground.

Wales has witnessed huge wildfires this summer, including one major incident and the evacuation of a village in Conwy county.

In the Rhinogydd mountain range in Gwynedd, which is home to a National Nature Reserve and a Special Area of Conservation, a blaze burned for nearly two weeks and affected over 2,000 acres.

Both fires were visible from space.

Meanwhile, a fire in Blaenavon, Torfaen, could be smelt as far away as Cardiff.

Although fewer wildfires were reported in the second half of July in England and Wales compared with 2025, Thomas said: "This year seems to have been worse, I would say, than any of the ones I can remember.

"I would expect this to probably be the worst year for wildfires perhaps we've ever had."

While some areas will recover quite quickly - potentially within a couple of years - he said: "It all depends on how deep the fire goes.

"If a fire burns into the soil and incinerates the soil... then you've lost hundreds of years worth of soil.

"So it's going to take hundreds of years really for that vegetation to come back in a similar way to what it was."

News.title: Veteran camps in woods for months waiting for home
News.content:
An Army veteran has spent the last 15 weeks camping in woods while waiting for his social housing application to be processed.

Blair Murray, 44, served more than a decade in the Royal Logistics Corps up to 2010, but was made homeless by a landlord last year and spent months staying with friends before setting up camp in woodland near Crook in County Durham.

Murray said he had lined up a job and arranged to start counselling sessions, but both were being held up by his lack of a home.

Since the BBC got in touch with Durham County Council, homeless prevention manager Christopher Hepworth said the authority had worked with the Armed Forces Outreach Service and booked him into a hotel.

Hepworth said: "We will continue to work with him to secure suitable, stable, long-term accommodation."

In the most recent survey carried out by the Office for Veterans' Affairs, one in 400 ex-service personnel reported they were homeless or sleeping rough.

A TV boss once responsible for The Great British Bake Off is suing Sky and her former employer, claiming that she was fired after voicing concerns over the treatment of the Bake Off brand.

Letty Kavanagh – formerly the managing director of Bake Off production company Love Productions – began legal proceedings in the High Court on Thursday (6 August) against both companies over her dismissal in November 2025.

She is also seeking an employment tribunal for wrongful dismissal and gender discrimination.

As reported by The Times, Kavanagh, who had been working at Love Productions for 18 years, claims that she was unfairly dismissed by Sky after raising alarms over its attempt to influence the business.

open image in gallery Kavanagh was the managing director of Love Productions, the company behind ‘Bake Off’ ( Channel 4 )

Specifically, Kavanagh says she expressed concern over potential plans at Sky, which purchased Love Productions in 2014, to air Bake Off on its own network.

Initially airing on the BBC, the cake-making competition series moved to Channel 4 in 2017; the broadcast deal was up for renewal in 2024, although Kavanagh claims that Sky, Netflix and Disney were all eyeing up a purchase of the format.

She alleges that she internally shared worries over the show moving to Sky, and that this could be a conflict of interest and impact the Love Productions brand, as well as reported plans by Sky to strip back the Bake Off franchise, cancelling the celebrity and junior versions, cutting hundreds of jobs in the process.

Kavanagh says that attempts to raise concerns with Sky’s senior management were dismissed, and that Sky retaliated by terminating her contract and “marching her out of the building” (as per Deadline).

open image in gallery Kavanagh alleges that Sky were considering moving ‘Bake Off’ from Channel 4 to its own network in 2024 ( Channel 4/Love Productions )

Speaking to the publication, an insider familiar with the case said that “Letty was unfairly dismissed by Sky for raising genuine concerns about its mismanagement of Love Productions – the creator of Bake Off”.

They continued: “She was looking out for staff and freelancers at the production company, who risk losing their jobs because of bad management decisions, and was trying to protect the public service broadcasting content which Love Productions is so famed for producing. In retaliation, she was fired.”

In her discrimination claims, Kavanagh alleges that male colleagues received better treatment on their departures from Love Productions. She claims that Sky have not paid her the money she is owed, “despite male colleagues receiving payouts”.

Rejecting any claims the company acted inappropriately, a Sky spokesperson said it would robustly defend Kavanagh’s legal claims.

In a statement, they said: “We do not recognise Ms Kavanagh’s account of events. We reject the possibility of a conflict of interest in relation to assets we control and wholly own and refute her allegations of discrimination and retaliation in the strongest possible terms.

“Regrettably, this matter is the subject of ongoing legal proceedings, in which we intend to vigorously defend our position.”
