World.title: L’Europe veut sortir de sa dépendance à Palantir
World.content:
"Soyons honnêtes, le produit de Palantir est très bon et addictif, c’est un peu comme le sucre dans le Coca", reconnaît le député MoDem Philippe Latombe, défenseur français de la souveraineté numérique. "Palantir est capable de traiter d’énormes quantités de données avec une grande précision et, grâce à son expérience, l’entreprise a eu le temps d’améliorer ses algorithmes auprès de nombreux clients et de les adapter à de nombreux cas d’utilisation."

Pourtant, la volonté de se libérer de Palantir gagne tout le continent : de Madrid, où le gouvernement de Pedro Sánchez a ordonné aux entreprises publiques d’exclure Palantir des futurs marchés publics, jusqu’aux services de renseignement intérieurs français (DGSI), qui ont préféré l’entreprise française ChapsVision à Palantir. Au Royaume-Uni, le prochain test pourrait avoir lieu en février 2027, lorsque le nouveau gouvernement travailliste d’Andy Burnham devra décider s’il met fin au contrat de 330 millions de livres sterling conclu avec Palantir pour la plateforme fédérée de données de la Sécurité sociale (NHS).

La décision prise le mois dernier par les services de renseignement français et allemands d’opter pour ChapsVision a porté un double coup dur à la direction de Palantir. Le PDG du géant américain, Alex Karp, est toutefois resté sûr de lui après ce revirement soudain, affirmant qu’il ne s’inquiétait pas de la concurrence européenne. "Nous avons un exemple de ce qui ne fonctionne pas", a-t-il ironisé la semaine dernière sur Fox Business. "Ça s'appelle l'Europe."

Alex Karp, PDG de Palantir, est l'invité de l'émission « The Claman Countdown » aux studios de Fox Business Network. | John Lamparski/Getty Images

Olivier Dellenbach, fondateur et PDG de ChapsVision, concède à POLITICO que son entreprise avait tiré profit de ce qu’il qualifie de "rejet viscéral de Palantir" en Europe.

Il refuse toutefois que ChapsVision soit réduit à une simple alternative anti-Palantir. La souveraineté numérique, affirme-t-il, restera une formule creuse si les gouvernements ne la transforment pas en politique industrielle. "Il faut plus de commandes publiques", estime Olivier Dellenbach.

La Belgique, l'Allemagne, le Luxembourg, la Roumanie, les Pays-Bas et le Canada ont déjà manifesté leur intérêt pour le système d'IA "Artemis" de l'armée française, selon Patrick Moreau, l'un des architectes de cette solution développée par l'entreprise française d'aérospatiale et de défense Thales.

World.title: France will test crisis response with 2027 blackout drill
World.content:
Its purpose will be to determine how the country would respond to a paralyzing electricity outage of the kind that hit Spain and Portugal in April 2025, or a major cyberattack targeting the power grid as Poland experienced last year — an act of sabotage Brussels has attributed to Russian intelligence services.

The simulation will test “the country's ability to respond," said one person familiar with preparations for the exercise, adding that it is intended to assess the time needed to restore power and the country’s ability to ensure the continuity of essential services.

The exercise was formally confirmed during an interministerial committee on national resilience on July 8. A detailed announcement should come before the end of the year.

The meeting notes outline other priorities, such as making sure the French state maintains access to goods considered "essential to ensuring the continuity of the state and the protection of the population."

These include “emergency blankets, generators, medicines, telecommunications equipment, equipment for law enforcement, as well as rare and critical raw materials.”

Stress test

Crisis preparedness has turned into a political issue in France as record-breaking heat and wildfires are forcing the country to reckon with its ability to respond to emergencies.

World.title: 31 days of solitude: Welcome to Brussels in August
World.content:
Older readers may remember when in 2017 — back when the EU was entirely in black and white — then-European Parliament President Antonio Tajani wrote to Commission chief Jean-Claude Juncker to point out that the Parliament was taking its summer break, and that no work should be sent over before early September. Tajani’s note was dated July 13.

A note from our Irony Department: This column is off next week as I’m on vacation. Although, as Tuscany is out of my price range, I’ll be vacationing at the Schuman roundabout instead.

But if major events happening while you’re on a beach or halfway up an Alp is a bad look, the alternative — working all through the summer just in case something happens — isn’t much better.

In the hot summer of 2009, when Tajani — yes, him again — was merely the European transport commissioner, he drew the short straw of running the good ship Berlaymont while the other commissioners took a break. He then used the time to remind Europeans not to lose their luggage, describing the “phenomenon” of lost luggage as “very important” and “extremely worrying.” Tajani, of course, was a close ally of the late Italian leader Silvio Berlusconi, who had an awful lot of baggage (maybe even 10,000 suitcases full a day).

The summer before Tajani’s plea to keep a closer eye on your suitcases, the EU had launched a bloc-wide labeling scheme for sunscreen. Günter Verheugen, the commissioner for industry at the time, called the scheme an example of “responsible business behavior.” And Verheugen had perhaps more of a need for sunscreen than most, as in 2006, photographs had emerged of him relaxing on a nudist beach in Lithuania wearing nothing but a baseball cap — oh, and he was with his chief of staff.

World.title: Germany’s hot topic this summer: A chancellor swap
World.content:
Ahead of crucial regional elections in September — in which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has a realistic chance of taking power in a German state for the first time — there is increasingly open discussion of a Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap, in the fall.

Public criticism has mainly come from those ousted from government in the reshuffle. But behind the scenes, a growing number of politicians from Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are discussing what would, by German standards, be a remarkable scenario: replacing the leader after little more than a year in the job.

Europe’s biggest economy has long been one of its most stable democracies, with no history of rattling through leaders like postwar Italy or post-Brexit Britain.

But the expected success of the AfD, in elections in which the CDU is expected to lose ground, is upending the country’s conventional political dynamics.

The theory behind a Kanzlertausch is that the conservatives will need to stem the fallout from the eastern elections and give themselves a boost by replacing a leader unable to shake his rock-bottom ratings.

But the stakes are high. The AfD — now the most popular party in national polls — would seek to capitalize on further coalition unrest. Replacing a chancellor years before the end of his term would mean venturing into largely uncharted political territory.

World.title: UK Labour membership plummeted under Keir Starmer
World.content:
Starmer faced a tricky 2025 after winning a landslide victory the previous year, which brought the center-left party back into power after 14 years.

He was forced into a series of policy U-turns by his party, and sacked Peter Mandelson as U.K. ambassador to the U.S. after fresh details on the closeness of his friendship with convicted sex-trafficker Jeffrey Epstein emerged.

Membership swelled under Starmer’s predecessor Jeremy Corbyn, with the party recording more than half a million Labour members at the peak of his popularity.

But under Starmer and his Chancellor Rachel Reeves, the party moved rightwards economically and on issues such as immigration and benefit payments, and expelled left-leaning party stalwarts such as Corbyn and Diane Abbott.

Such changes put the leadership at odds with its members, sections of whom are notably more left wing than the British public at large. The removal of the whip from several Labour MPs for voting against government welfare policies in 2024, and again in 2025, were watershed moments.

In 2023, Starmer told members: “If you don’t like the changes that we’ve made, I say the door is open, and you can leave.”

World.title: "A shame for Portugal": Israeli ambassador urges cancellation of Kanye West concert in Algarve
World.content:
The Embassy of Israel in Portugal has criticised Kanye West's concert, scheduled for this Friday in the Algarve, and has called for the show to be cancelled, citing the artist's public statements, deemed antisemitic and supportive of Adolf Hitler and Nazism.

 

"Someone who glorified Hitler, promoted antisemitism and claimed that slavery was a choice, a remark that deeply offended millions of descendants of slavery's victims. This is not provocation, it is hate speech," says ambassador Oren Rozenblat in a video posted on social media.

In a statement, the ambassador recalled comments by the musician in which he said he "liked Hitler" and that he was "a Nazi", accusing him of glorifying the Nazi regime, promoting antisemitism and offending communities affected by racism and slavery. The embassy argues that these statements go beyond mere provocation and constitute hate speech.

Rozenblat points out that other countries have already taken measures against the artist performing or entering their territories, arguing that "a democratic society should not give a platform to someone who glorifies Hitler, promotes Nazism and defends antisemitism".

The Embassy of Israel in Portugal also says it has asked the mayor of Faro for the cancellation of the concert and urges citizens not to attend, arguing that going ahead with the show would be "a disgrace for Portugal and for the Portuguese".

Would you buy a ticket for an artist who promoted hatred against Black people, against Muslims, against Christians or against LGBT people? If the answer is no, why should it be any different when the target is Jews? Embaixador de Israel em Portugal, Oren Rozenblat

The Israeli ambassador in Portugal stresses that the issue is not about people's positions on Israel, but about what he considers to be statements of hatred against Jews.

He also questions whether the Portuguese would buy tickets for an artist who encouraged attacks against other communities, such as Black people, Muslims, Christians or LGBT people, insisting that the same principle should apply to antisemitism.

"A non-issue"

Torcato Jorge, CEO and co-founder of Raya Culture, the event organiser, said earlier, in an interview with Euronews, that cancelling Kanye West's concert is "a non-issue", driven by "disinformation".

"It is a music event that is going ahead. It would become an issue if the security services identified a national threat to public order, which is not the case," he reiterates.

The organiser expressed confidence that all the conditions are in place for the concert to go ahead and says that the organisation has complied with the law from day one. "The SIS has not identified the artist, or in this case the US citizen, as a national threat or a terrorist," he notes. "There has to be an internal state security report saying that this citizen cannot enter the country," he adds.

Speaking to Euronews, the CEO acknowledges that the issue is becoming "a political matter". "Each country is free to decide whether or not to allow a citizen to enter, but within the European Union no country has vetoed his entry into its national territory."

Controversial statements and cancelled concerts

In recent years, Kanye West has been at the centre of various international controversies, mainly because of comments considered antisemitic and because of contentious behaviour, including episodes linked to sexist attitudes, such as the case involving his wife, Bianca Censori, at the Grammys.

Although he has apologised for some of his comments, the European tour of the rapper, who also goes by the stage name Ye, has run into difficulties, with concerts cancelled in several countries.

In the United Kingdom, three performances at the Wireless festival, scheduled for July, were cancelled after the country revoked the rapper's permission to enter. In France, the artist himself postponed a concert scheduled for Marseille after criticism from local authorities.

Poland also cancelled a show planned for June, citing legal and formal reasons, after the minister of culture criticised the rapper's antisemitic statements. In Switzerland, FC Basel decided not to go ahead with a concert planned for its stadium, stating that it did not want to give the artist a platform.

In Italy, Kanye West also had a concert cancelled. The show, scheduled for July in Reggio Emilia, was banned by the local authorities because of concerns about security and public order, in particular the potential for protests and unrest. Rapper Travis Scott also had a concert cancelled in the same Italian city.

World.title: Cyprus energy minister: Meridiam's entry into Great Sea Interconnector is 'vote of confidence'
World.content:
Nicosia has expressed its satisfaction at the entry of the French investment group Meridiam as majority shareholder in the Great Sea Interconnector.

 

Cyprus’ Energy Minister, Michalis Damianou, said that the participation of the French group gives new momentum to the project’s implementation and confirms the shared political will of Cyprus and Greece to advance electricity interconnection.

He added that the Republic of Cyprus is still awaiting the due diligence study of the European Investment Bank (EIB) before deciding whether it will participate in the project as a shareholder.

Damianou described Meridiam’s entry as a "vote of confidence" in the project, while noting that the government’s final decisions will be based on the findings of the European Investment Bank, which will also determine the project’s final cost.

The agreement for the entry of the French investment group Meridiam as majority shareholder in the company Great Sea Interconnector (GSI) was signed on Thursday in Athens.

According to the initial plan, the company, a subsidiary of IPTO, will take on the development of the Greece–Cyprus electricity interconnection project.

Meridiam’s participation in GSI’s share capital is expected to significantly strengthen the project, as it brings international know-how and strong investment credibility, reinforcing the company’s strategic objective: connecting Cyprus to the European electricity system via Greece and boosting the energy security and resilience of both countries.

A tripartite agreement was also signed between IPTO, GSI and Nexans. The three parties will work together from day one to accelerate the works, with priority given to completing seabed surveys.

Meridiam is a leading international investor, developer and operator of infrastructure projects, based in Paris and with a strong presence in Europe, the United States and Africa.

It specialises in strategically important public infrastructure projects, which it develops, finances, delivers and manages with a long-term investment horizon, in close cooperation with governments, regulators and public bodies.

At the same time, the process to approve financing of the project by the EIB is under way.

In parallel with this development, the Cyprus–Israel electricity interconnection is also progressing towards implementation.

IPTO, as the implementing body, has completed and will in the coming days send to the regulatory authorities of Cyprus and Israel the cost–benefit study, an important milestone for the project’s progress.

The project is expected to strengthen Greece’s role as a strategic energy hub linking the electricity systems of the Eastern Mediterranean with the European electricity market.

World.title: Military shake-up poses little threat to Ukraine's ongoing drone revolution
World.content:
Zigzagging between robots, weapons and computers in his garage workshop, Ukrainian engineer Eduard Trotsenko was bubbling with excitement as he showed off his latest prototypes and dreamed of sci-fi-inspired futuristic ideas.

 

Top of his ideas list are "mechanical birds" that can land on high-voltage power lines and recharge themselves, and "robot dogs" that can be sent into battle.

"In order to save human lives, to save soldiers, there must be robots," Trotsenko told the AFP news agency.

Autonomous weapons have come to dominate the war with Russia.

Aerial drones are used on the front lines for reconnaissance and to drop explosives, while down below ground robots support logistics operations.

Ukraine has built a sprawling drone industry from scratch, hailed by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the best in the world.

Soldiers from Ukraine's Khartia brigade load ammunition onto a combat ground drone bound for the front line in Kharkiv region, 27 January, 2026 AP Photo

But the dismissal last month of popular defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, one of the most ardent backers of drones, raised some concerns over the future of the sector.

"I don't understand why they sacked Fedorov," Trotsenko, the founder and CEO of robot manufacturer Temerland, said.

Despite his removal, industry players and military personnel AFP spoke to said there was no going back now.

"The young people there won't let it go. There'll definitely be drones," Trotsenko said.

Into the kill zone

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, 55-year-old Trotsenko switched from making car charging stations to military robots.

His speciality is ground drones: autonomous vehicles that crawl the "kill zone," the kilometres-deep stretch of territory where Russian and Ukrainian drones lurk in the skies, posing a constant danger to anybody below.

For now, they mainly help evacuate wounded soldiers from the battlefield or ferry supplies, reducing the need to send more men into the kill zone.

But Trotsenko is looking at combat prototypes: one equipped with an RPG rocket launcher, the other with a heavy machine gun, controlled by onboard artificial intelligence (AI).

Ukraine's former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov speaks in Kyiv, 1 July, 2026 AP Photo

"They're currently being tested in some brigades," said Trotsenko, who is awaiting a green light for further rollout by the General Staff.

Fedorov had been crucial to pushing the technological shift within Ukraine's army.

He created the Defence AI Center A1, a hub dedicated to embedding AI in the military and using live feedback from the front to speed up the deployment of new technology.

Fedorov also pushed to bring private companies into the military system, putting competition at the heart of the army's innovation.

"In a private company, you can take risks more quickly," said Trotsenko, explaining how small companies were incentivised to modify and adapt at speed to win contracts.

'Bottom-up'

Hundreds of kilometres away, a 45-year-old military commander who goes by the call sign "Jason", was just back from a mission.

He heads a unit that operates the kind of ground drones that Trotsenko develops in his garage.

"You can afford to lose a drone, but not a person. The probability of human losses there is reduced," he told AFP.

That kind of mantra, using drones to save lives, was precisely what Fedorov had been pushing at the defence ministry.

Soldiers from Ukraine's Khartia brigade operate drones from the Kharkiv region, 30 February, 2026 AP Photo

After he was sacked, protestors forced out the Soviet-style commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrsky, who had clashed with Fedorov's reform drive, criticising him for not embracing drones and being too careless with soldiers' lives.

Asked whether Fedorov's removal could upset Ukraine's drone development, Jason brushes it off.

"It's not that simple...the technological initiative was not flowing from the top down. It wasn't a government order," he said.

After Russia invaded, "there was an explosion of bottom-up initiative."

Young engineers began to create new products, showed them to the military, who took what they wanted and then started their own development, he said.

Now, programmers, telecoms specialists and engineers are fully integrated into the army.

Jason said "the shortage of professionally trained people" is the biggest challenge he faces.

Back in Trotsenko's workshop, his engineers are already working to redefine the technological and geographical limits of war.

On a whiteboard, he sketched out his vision of the future: conflicts fought by "humanoid robots", controlled by operators in another country, or wounded soldiers lying in hospital beds.

"Things have really taken off," he said confidently.

World.title: Portugal: next week starts with sharp drop in fuel prices
World.content:
New week, new prices: from 10 August, industry forecasts point to a sharp drop in fuel prices, of around 12 cents on diesel and 12.5 cents on petrol, according to the Automobile Club of Portugal (ACP) (source in Portuguese).

 

If the forecasts for next week are confirmed, the average price of diesel will fall to 1.931 euros per litre, while petrol will retreat to 1.855 euros per litre.

These figures may still change, the ACP notes, since "this forecast consists of average values based on crude prices at last Thursday's market close", that is, "if there are fluctuations in crude and fuel prices up to the end of this Friday, there may be some variation in prices compared with what is currently forecast".

This Friday, regular diesel is costing 2.051 euros per litre, while 95-octane unleaded petrol is at 1.980 euros per litre, according to the average prices published by the Directorate-General for Energy and Geology ( (source in Portuguese)DGEG (source in Portuguese)) (source in Portuguese).

According to the same source, these daily average prices "are calculated on the basis of the prices reported by filling stations, weighted by the quantities sold in the latest period for which figures are available, incorporating discounts applied at forecourts such as fleet cards and others".

The prices charged to end consumers may vary from station to station, since this sector, and consequently its pricing policy, is liberalised.

Fuel prices continue to be heavily affected by the war in the Middle East, with the US, Israel and Iran involved in military attacks in the region. The war has led to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of the world's oil and natural gas passes, causing major swings in fuel prices.

Since the outbreak of the war in the Middle East, the government has undertaken to apply a new extraordinary and temporary cut in the ISP fuel tax whenever there is an increase in fuel prices of more than 10 cents, in order to mitigate the surge in prices.

It is therefore expected that the government will adjust the ISP discount, as has been happening in recent weeks, which may lead to changes in the estimated prices from next Monday.

World.title: Uzbekistan-developed AI module launches aboard Earth observation satellite
World.content:
A Chinese hyperspectral Earth observation satellite carrying an artificial intelligence module developed by Uzbek engineers has entered orbit as part of a joint project between China's STAR.VISION and Uzbekistan's national space agency, Uzcosmos.

 

The mission marks the first deployment of an AI module developed by Uzbek engineers aboard one of STAR.VISION's international satellite projects.

Successfully Launches the Samarkand-2028 Hyperspectral Satellite into Orbit

The satellite, named Samarkand-2028, lifted off on 5 August from a sea-based launch platform near Haiyang in China's Shandong Province.

China's Shandong Province. Uzcosmos

Explaining the satellite's name, Uzbekistan's Minister of Digital Technologies, Sherzod Shermatov, wrote on social media: "The name Samarkand-2028 is no coincidence. Samarkand earned the right to host the 2028 International Astronautical Congress, marking the first time the world's largest space congress will be held in Central Asia."

The satellite collects hyperspectral imagery, recording data across multiple wavelengths of light.

Compared with conventional satellite imagery, this provides a more detailed picture of the Earth's surface, making it useful for applications requiring precise environmental analysis.

AI processes imagery in orbit

The AI module processes part of the satellite's imagery while it is still in orbit, analysing the data before transmission rather than sending all of the raw information to Earth.

According to Uzcosmos, this reduces the volume of data transmitted to ground stations while improving the speed and efficiency of image analysis.

"This enables faster results, reduces the volume of data that needs to be transmitted, and makes analysis on the ground more efficient," Shermatov wrote.

Rather than functioning solely as an imaging platform, the satellite can carry out part of the analytical work in space, allowing ground teams to receive more readily usable information.

Onboard AI is becoming an increasingly important capability in Earth observation missions as satellite operators seek to manage growing volumes of data more efficiently and shorten the time between image capture and analysis.

Related Uzbekistan prepares for first homegrown satellite and astronaut mission

Processing data before it reaches Earth

Earth observation satellites generate vast amounts of data, placing significant demands on communications systems and ground infrastructure.

Processing part of that data onboard allows only the most relevant information to be transmitted, reducing bandwidth requirements and speeding up access to imagery.

Hyperspectral imaging is increasingly used in agriculture, environmental monitoring and natural resource management because it can detect changes in vegetation, soil and water that are difficult to identify using conventional optical imagery.

In agriculture, it can help identify crop stress before visible signs appear, while environmental agencies can use it to monitor land degradation, water quality and ecosystem changes.

The technology also has applications in natural resource assessment, disaster response and urban planning.

Satellite launch process Uzcosmos

Building a broader space partnership

The launch follows a strategic cooperation agreement signed by Uzcosmos and STAR.VISION in 2025 to develop Earth observation technologies and expand collaboration in satellite development.

Uzbekistan is also preparing to launch a 6U CubeSat in 2028 while developing the framework for a 10 to 14-day astronaut mission in cooperation with international partners.

World.title: Surprise discovery as ancient domus uncovered beneath restoration site in Rome
World.content:
What began as a routine engineering project on Rome's Caelian Hill has turned into one of the city's most significant recent archaeological discoveries.

 

Architects reinforcing an ancient Roman wall at Villa Celimontana unexpectedly uncovered the remains of a large Roman-era building decorated with elaborate mosaics, frescoes and painted ceilings. Archaeologists have so far identified eight rooms, five of which have been fully excavated, while several more extend beyond the current excavation area.

Chief archaeologist Simona Moretta said the team expected ancient remains given the site's location close to the Roman Forum, but not on such a scale.

"Being in the heart of ancient Rome, a stone's throw from the Roman Forum, that there could be something ancient, we had certainly taken that possibility into account, but certainly not with this importance. We have found a building with five full rooms, but another eight rooms whose walls enter into the area of excavation section but that we could not excavate. So it is a rather large building, especially with valuable surface decorations, because we have, in particular, in the room 'V', we have superimposed two mosaics - one from the third century (AD) and the lower one instead is from the second (century AD)."

Excavation teams are now cleaning and cataloguing hundreds of artefacts, including marble fragments, ceramics, mosaics and painted plaster. Restorers are also reconstructing a richly decorated ceiling recovered in large sections.

Moretta said the preservation of the ceiling exceeded expectations.

"We also have some pieces of frescoes and, especially on the most recent mosaic we have found in this room, we have found the painted ceiling of the room in large parts that we have been able to sort through with the very good restorers."

She added: "We have now put it in storage and then it will be reconstructed, I think we will have more than 50% of the entire room. A beautiful ceiling painted in red and blue circles with white stucco frames with denticles."

The discovery forced engineers to expand what had originally been planned as a straightforward stabilisation project. Architect Alessandra Centroni, director of works, said the excavation quickly became far more extensive than anticipated.

"Clearly, this being an exceptional discovery, we deepened the excavation that was not planned for this, of this entity, but we gradually went deeper, precisely to try to understand what we had in front of us, in short, what were we discovering."

According to Daniela Porro, Special Superintendent of Rome for Archaeology, the complex dates to the second century AD and was later modified during the third century.

"There are eight rooms, of which five are completely excavated, three partially excavated, which, however, have given us back a decoration of great value with floor mosaics. One of these rooms has a beautiful, geometric mosaic, within the centre there is an emblem depicting a dolphin and fish around a crater."

Researchers have not yet determined the building's original purpose. Its refined decoration suggests it may have belonged to an influential Roman family, although another possibility is that it served as barracks connected to the city's ancient fire brigade.

Porro said further research will be needed before any firm conclusions can be drawn.

"It could probably have been a domus belonging to an important family, that would have such an elegant decoration, or it could also be barracks linked to the fire brigade of ancient Rome. And on this point, the studies are still going on and certainly they will eventually tell us something more."

The excavation forms part of restoration work funded through Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), supported by the European Union. Archaeologists expect ongoing excavation and conservation work to provide new insights into the history of ancient Rome.

World.title: Danube: Wehrmacht soldiers and WWII motorbike recovered after 80 years
World.content:
In the harbour you would normally see boats moored, but in Budapest a motorbike from the Second World War has now been recovered from the middle of the Danube. On the riverbed at the level of Budapest there are more relics: two soldiers have also been exhumed from the muddy riverbed, according to the Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge (German War Graves Commission).

 

According to its own account, the Volksbund sent a reburial specialist to Budapest, who carried out the exhumation with the help of Hungarian colleagues. Alongside the soldiers’ remains, which were preserved by the mud, numerous German Tellermine 35 anti-tank mines were also found. These were used against tanks during the Second World War.

The motorbike was discovered on 2 August on the Buda side of the Hungarian parliament, next to the harbour at Batthyány Square. Volksbund

Because the harbour mud on the bed of the Danube at Batthyány Square is mixed with gas oil, it has created ideal conditions for preserving wrecks and human remains. The reburial specialist said, according to the Volksbund, that it was thanks to this petroleum product that the mud had also preserved the identity discs exceptionally well, so that letters and numbers are still clearly legible.

What is known about the soldiers from the Danube

The identity discs served as the soldiers’ ID at the time. Each soldier carried a disc in duplicate. In the event of death, one half was sent to the Wehrmacht information office, which could then inform family members.

In the case of the soldiers recovered from the Danube, their identity discs are still fully legible, according to the Volksbund. Both halves are still together, which means the report of their death never reached the information office in Berlin.

After examination, the soldiers are to be buried at the Budaörs war cemetery on the outskirts of Budapest.

The motorbike was recovered by staff from the Institute and Museum of Military History. They believe it is a DKW NZ 350-1 model, which at the time was regarded as particularly robust and reliable, according to the Volksbund.

A petrol can is also among the objects found on the exposed riverbed of the Danube. Volksbund

A military decoration from the Second World War and a petrol can were also recovered. The remains had been lying on the bed of the Danube for around 80 years.

More recoveries possible if low water persists

Because water levels are extremely low, the Volksbund expects shipwrecks to emerge from which war dead could be recovered. Hungary would initially be responsible, but if there is evidence of possible German war dead, the Volksbund will be notified and may be involved.

World.title: Testosterone and fertility: the trade-off men aren't told about
World.content:
Testosterone is trending in gyms, on social online and in politics. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth even wants troops screened for low testosterone. But taking supplements can shut down the body's natural production.

Making sperm is, in large part, what testosterone is for. Which is why it is ironic when a man who doesn't need it starts taking it anyway: His brain registers an unusually high level of the hormone in his blood, concludes his body has made too much, and sends the order to stop. The testes go silent and sperm production declines.

Testosterone is having a moment. It is all over social media, gym culture and wellness forums, sold by online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services. The information surrounding it ranges from oversimplified to outright dangerous. Men are taking more of it than ever, in pursuit of feeling more like men. In doing so, they may be telling their bodies to stop producing it themselves.

Here is what the science says — what testosterone does, who genuinely needs treatment, and what it can cost the men who take it without needing it.

How does taking testosterone stop sperm production?

Your body regulates testosterone the way a thermostat regulates heat. When the brain detects abnormally high levels of the hormone in the bloodstream, it sends a signal to the testes to stop producing it naturally. The testes effectively go offline, and because sperm production depends on what happens inside them, that shuts down too.

Some men who self-medicate with testosterone push their levels to more than four times the clinical lower threshold. The consequences include blood clotting disorders, cardiovascular stress, mood instability and, in some cases, irreversible fertility damage. What's sold as a shortcut to strength and libido can, unsupervised, cost a man his fertility.

What are normal testosterone levels by age?

Testosterone peaks during puberty, typically between 13 and 15. After that, it declines slowly for the rest of a man's life. A lower level at 40 than at 15 isn't a disorder — its aging.

What counts as low testosterone?

The threshold that doctors use is 300 nanograms per deciliter of blood.

But this threshold comes with a condition: It must be confirmed by at least two blood tests taken at different times of the day, because levels fluctuate.

Below that number, a doctor may begin to consider treatment. Above 300, there is no clinical basis for intervention.

How can you increase testosterone naturally?

Before any medical treatment is considered, four key lifestyle factors should be examined: sleep, alcohol consumption, smoking and drug use, and chronic stress. Each of these has a measurable impact on testosterone levels. Addressing them may be all that's needed and carries none of the risks of hormonal therapy.

What is testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) and who actually needs it?

Testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, treats a diagnosed hormonal deficiency. It's a legitimate medical procedure — involving injections, pills, creams — that works for men who need it.

But plenty of men taking it don't have that deficiency. Men with normal testosterone levels are increasingly seeking TRT out anyway, not as a treatment but as a performance enhancer. They're getting it from unregulated online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services that write prescriptions without adequate medical assessment.

Can testosterone therapy cause permanent infertility?

In some cases, yes.

Men who stop taking testosterone are likely to recover their own production within months. But not all of them. Depending on the dose and how long a man has been using, research puts the share who never recover at somewhere between one in ten and one in five.

Low testosterone: What it does to men's health To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Does testosterone therapy actually work – or is it a placebo?

Many men who self-administer testosterone report feeling stronger, sharper and more energetic. Some of that may reflect genuine physiological change.

A significant portion is likely the placebo effect — a well-documented human tendency to feel better when we believe we are being treated. That does not make the feeling less real. It does mean that unsupervised hormonal intervention is a high-risk gamble for a benefit that may exist entirely in one's mind.

The bottom line

Doctors' advice is unambiguous: Get tested, know the number, and treat everything else — the websites, the influencers, the gym contacts — as anecdote, not medicine.

A lot of men aren't waiting. Chasing peak masculinity online, they're reaching for the one substance that could tell their own bodies to stop making it.

Edited by: Kaukab Shairani

World.title: Is it really the hottest day ever?
World.content:
Every time a new heat record is broken, skepticism follows. How do scientists know a day or a summer was really the hottest on record or that a heat wave was historic? DW has the answers.

Another summer, another wave of headlines about record-breaking heat. From Northeast Asia to Europe to the United States, extreme temperatures are contributing to thousands of deaths, fueling wildfires and straining water, food and energy supplies.

But what do the words behind the headlines mean? How do scientists know if temperatures are record-breaking? Why do cities warm up more than rural areas? And does humidity really make everything feel hotter?

DW spoke to climatologists to answer some common questions about how heat is measured, and why understanding heat terminology matters for everyone.

What does 'record-breaking heat' mean anyway?

It depends on what's being compared. Thousands of weather stations around the world track temperatures. A location can set a record if its temperature exceeds the previous high recorded at the station for a specific day, month or season.

Scientists also calculate regional and global temperature records by combining data from weather stations, ships and ocean buoys and determining the average across larger areas.

How far back that comparison goes depends on the dataset. The oldest continuous record of temperatures in the world is the Central England Temperature Data Series, which started in 1659.

The 10 warmest years in modern global record-keeping have all occurred within the past decade Image: Thorsten Wagner/W2Art/picture alliance

But the three most complete datasets — maintained by the United States' Goddard Institute for Space Studies and National Centers for Environmental Information, plus the United Kingdom's Met Office Hadley Centre — began recording comprehensively in 1880.

These are the datasets behind statements such as "the past decade was the warmest on record." When media outlets use the shorthand "hottest day ever," they are talking about recording temperatures.

While Earth has experienced hotter climates and extreme temperatures over its 4.5-billion-year history, today's warming is exceptional in the context of the 12,000 years of human civilization.

But how do scientists know about Earth's climate before humans and thermometers were around?

To understand Earth's earlier climate, scientists rely on natural records known as "climate archives" that help them recreate long-term patterns in temperature. Those include ice cores, tree rings, ocean sediments and fossils.

"These preserve information about past temperatures, rainfall and atmospheric conditions going back thousands to millions of years," Friedrike Otto, a climatologist and founder of research group World Weather Attribution (WWA), told DW in an email.

The most complete continuous ice core record, drilled in Antarctica, stretches back more than a million years, for example. It contains ancient air bubbles that allow researchers to measure past atmospheric carbon dioxide levels. But other "climate archives" stretch back much further.

"As we know the equations that govern the physics of the climate, we can also use climate models to see how changes in different drivers produce different climate and weather conditions," said Otto.

That's helped scientists discern that higher greenhouse gases are closely linked with warmer global temperatures throughout Earth's history. For instance, about 56 million years ago, large amounts of carbon entered the atmosphere, likely from volcanic activity and methane released from ocean sediments, triggering a major period of global heating.

The difference today is climate change is primarily caused by humans burning fossil fuels and is happening at a much faster rate than over the last million years or so, says NASA.

But how do scientists know if heat waves are a trend or an anomaly?

Climate scientists analyze decades of data to distinguish long-term climatic changes from normal weather fluctuations. A single hot year doesn't prove a trend. But as records grow longer, statistical analyses and climate models make it easier to identify persistent patterns.



"You're looking for consistency. You're looking for a convergence of all the evidence," said Gerald Mills, a climatologist at University College Dublin.

How to deal with a heatstroke To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scientific agencies across different continents — including NASA, NOAA and the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service — track global temperatures, using different methods and data sets. Despite those differences, they've reached the same conclusion: there is a heating trend and that the last decade has produced the hottest years ever recorded.

Researchers also use attribution science to assess the role climate change plays in extreme weather. Using climate models, they compare the likelihood and intensity of an event in today's climate with a simulated world without human-caused warming.

WWA ran exactly that analysis on Europe's June 2026 heat wave. The scientists found it was the most severe on record for the region studied. In 1976, a famously hot year across Europe, those temperatures would have been virtually impossible.

What heat metrics should you pay attention to in a weather forecast?

Air temperature or "actual temperature" don't fully describe how heat affects the human body. That's why weather services also provide "feels like" figures, which account for other factors.

In the US, the National Weather Service's heat index is based on air temperature and humidity. The UK's Met Office's "feels like" temperature also factors in wind chill.

Why does high humidity make it feel hotter and why is a high wet bulb temperature dangerous?

High humidity means more moisture in the air, which makes it harder for sweat evaporate. That reduces the body's ability to cool down, so the air temperature feels hotter in humid conditions.

Scientists also use the wet bulb temperature as a measure for heat stress. It is recorded by wrapping the bulb of a thermometer in a damp cloth. As water evaporates from the cloth, the bulb cools and the temperature reading drops, similar to how evaporation of sweat cools the human body.

As the wet bulb temperature approaches the actual air temperature, the air becomes increasingly saturated, and the body struggles to cool itself, increasing the risk of dangerous heat stress.

At sustained wet bulb temperatures of around 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit), the body can overheat even if people are resting in the shade or staying hydrated. But dry heat can be dangerous too, considering the risk of dehydration.

Why are cities hotter than rural areas?

That's because of the urban heat island effect, which makes cities warmer than surrounding areas for a few reasons.

Cities often replace vegetation and trees with roads, buildings and other hard surfaces that absorb and store heat. Greenery, on the other hand, cools an area through shade and evaporation. Dense buildings and narrow streets in urban areas also reduce air ventilation.

"All those things together, depending on where you are in relation to the city, can make it quite uncomfortable," Mills said.

Planting more trees, adding parks and green roofs, unsealing paved areas where possible and using lighter-colored, more reflective building materials can all help reduce the urban heat island effect by increasing shade, evaporation and the reflection of sunlight.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

08/07/2026 August 7, 2026 CBI probe finds testing agency's own experts behind NEET paper leak

The Central Bureau of Investigation’s (CBI) has accused 13 people in the NEET-UG 2026 paper 'leak' case.

In its investigation, the CBI has concluded that the alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leak was a well-coordinated conspiracy which involved people from multiple states and had National Testing Agency's (NTA) own subject experts sell the question papers through a network of middlemen.

The 13 accused include three NTA subject experts, coaching operators, middlemen and candidates.

The CBI has alleged that the NTA's subject experts exploited their official roles to illegally access the examination papers before the test and circulate them through a network of intermediaries.

The accused have been booked under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the Prevention of Corruption Act and the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.

World.title: Thailand: Several killed in school shooting north of Bangkok
World.content:
The shooting incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi, just north of the capital city of Bangkok. Several people were killed in the attack.

Several people were killed and others injured in a shooting at a high school in Thailand's Nonthaburi province, north of the capital city of Bangkok, local authorities said.

Students, teachers and other workers were evacuated from school as authorities deployed police officers, rescue workers and emergency doctors to the scene.

Boy accused of killing grandparents before school shooting

According to the police, the suspected gunman, who is a 14-year-old student at the school, first fatally shot his grandparents with his grandfather's handgun. Then, he went to his school and killed three teachers and three students before killing himself.

Earlier, Thai national police spokesperson Trairong Phiwphan said that 15 people were wounded.

In a statement, police said the gunman fired 26 rounds, and an additional 34 rounds of ammunition were found at the scene.

Students, teachers and other staff members were evacuated from the school Image: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

Meanwhile, Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul expressed his condolences and stated that he had instructed relevant officials to assist those affected.

"It's such a terrible incident. It should never have happened. How could this happen in our country?" he told reporters.

Later, Anutin said that the teenage suspect in the deadly school shooting was "under stress" and had planned the attack. The prime minister also told reporters that he would discuss gun control with the country's police chief.

Students express shock

The incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi.

"I didn't think it was a gun at first," an 18-year-old student told Reuters, adding that he initially thought there were firecrackers. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. ​Then it started again."

Belongings left behind by evacuated students at Debsirin Nonthaburi School, following the shooting incident at the school Image: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

"I was afraid that I would die, and I was scared that I wouldn't be able to pursue my dreams," said Pawarisa Maylissa, a grade 12 student who hopes to attend medical school. "I heard many gunshots very loudly because it seemed the suspect was on the floor directly above us. I could even hear bullets hitting the floor."

According to district authorities, the Debsirin Nonthaburi School had an enrollment of around 3,100 students and 147 teachers in the 2025 academic year.

School shootings in Thailand

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. It is estimated that around 10 million firearms are in circulation, or about one for every seven people.

In February, a 17-year-old stole a gun from the police and opened fire at a public high school in southern Thailand. The two-hour attack resulted in one death and two injuries.

In October 2023, a 14-year-old opened fire at Bangkok's popular Siam Paragon shopping mall, killing two people and wounding five others. Police said the shooter used a modified pistol, originally designed to fire blanks, that had likely been bought online.

World.title: US judge orders Meta to pay $567 million over harm to children
World.content:
A New Mexico judge ruled Meta created a "public nuisance" that harmed children's mental health, ordering the company to pay over half a billion dollars in damages and overhaul safety features on Facebook and Instagram.

A judge in the US state of New Mexico has ordered Meta on Thursday to pay $567 million (€492 million) and overhaul how Facebook and Instagram operate for young users in the state.

Judge Bryan Biedscheid's ruling, issued in Santa Fe, states the company created a "public nuisance" that harmed children's mental health. It also comes on top of $375 million in damages a jury ordered against Meta in March, bringing the company's total New Mexico liability to $942 million. That March verdict found Meta violated the state's consumer protection law by misleading the public about the safety of its platforms for children.

Why smart glasses threaten privacy of women and children To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

State Attorney General Raul Torrez sued Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, in 2023. On Thursday, he said the ruling holds the company accountable for design choices that put children at risk.

"Today's decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online," he said.

What does the verdict entail?

Roughly three-quarters of the $567 million, to be paid out over five years, will fund mental health treatment for young people. The rest will go toward prevention programs, screening, and related services.

US jury fines Meta in landmark child‑safety case To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The judge also ordered Meta to make direct changes to Facebook and Instagram, including monthly limits on teen usage, tighter notification controls, stronger safeguards on adult contact with minors, oversight of AI chatbots, and improved handling of child sexual abuse reports.

The company must also work with schools to build a reporting system for flagging underage users, and must also delete data it holds on children under 13. Federal privacy law bars Meta from collecting personal data to verify children's ages, so the court instead ordered the company to keep improving its AI-based age-estimation tools.

How has Meta responded?

Meta has pledged to appeal the latest New Mexico verdict.

"We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content," the company said in a statement, adding: "We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts."

The new penalty, ableit massive, is still a small fraction of Meta's roughly $60 billion in annual profit. Investors have largely shrugged it off, with shares dipping less than half a percent in after-hours trading. However, the company still faces a wave of related lawsuits, including a trial set for later this month in Oakland, California, involving 29 states, and separate suits already underway or filed in several other states.

Australia's under-16s forced offline by social media ban To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Moreover, several countries are contemplating social media bans on children under the ages of 15 or 16 to limit the harm caused by being online, Australia — citing mental health, cyber bullying and concerns over lack of physical activity, among others — became the first nation to introduce such a ban for kids under 16 back in December.

Britain, Canada, Indonesia, Malaysia, Turkey and several European countries have also cracked down on teen use of social media.

World.title: Middle East: Houthi attack wounds 11 in Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels killed scores of Yemeni government troops in missile and drone attacks on Thursday and Friday, with France's AFP reporting 61 soldiers dead in multiple attacks.

A rebel spokesman said the attacks were in response to increased Saudi Arabian military support for Yemen's internationally recognized government and its forces.

Saudi Arabia's military backing of the Yemenis since 2015 and alliance with the US have marked it for attack by both the Houthis and Iran.

Thursday's ballistic missile and drone attacks injured dozens of troops beyond the 58 reported dead, in what Yemeni military sources called the worst attack on troops since 2022.

The Yemeni Ministry of Defense said in a statement that a military response would come, "at the appropriate place and time."

Thursday's attack occurred amid a series of air assaults, including one that wounded 11 civilians in the Najran region.

On Friday, three more troops were killed and four more injured when Houthis targeted Yemeni soldiers in Marib province.

The Red Sea and Yemen have become more hotly contested than ever since the Houthis leaned into the US-Iran war, helping Tehran leverage the situation in the Strait of Hormuz — and its impact on the global economy.

The expected joint defense agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan is a direct response to the changing security situation in the broader Middle East.

World.title: Argentina: Milei's property bill triggers protests, anger
World.content:
Police clashed with protesters in Buenos Aires after thousands rallied against President Javier Milei's private property bill. The government had already dropped a provision on foreigners buying land in Argentina.

Security forces used tear gas, rubber bullets and water cannons against demonstrators in downtown Buenos Aires on Thursday, eventually dispersing the crowd which was protesting a new law pushed by the government of President Javier Milei.

Several thousand demonstrators, mobilized by left-wing groups and labor unions, rallied outside the Argentine Senate against the "Inviolability of Private Property" bill, which is currently under debate.

Opponents of the property bill see the danger of 'colonization' Image: Luis Robayo/AFP

According to EFE news agency, the protest had been peaceful before police intervened. AFP news agency, however, reported that some protesters threw stones and other projectiles at officers.

Why are Argentinians opposing Milei's private property bill?

The new bill aims to streamline eviction procedures, change the rules on rural land use and install new limits on government seizing private property.

The proposal would have also raised the limit of land that could be owned by foreign buyers from 15% to 25%. Amid growing backlash, however, the ruling party removed the chapter on foreigners buying land.

Milei's government hopes the reform would help the country attract investment, but rivals of the libertarian leader warn against "colonization, fragmentation, fracture and balkanization" of Argentina.

On Thursday, protesters carried placards reading: "The homeland is not for sale."

"Defending our territory is crucial … We must take to the streets to protest. It is our Argentina that we must defend; it is not for sale," Marcela Arin, who traveled from the southern province of Neuquen to join the protest in Buenos Aires, told EFE.

Nearly 5% of Argentina's territory — an area similar in size to England — is already foreign- owned, according to a 2025 study by researchers from the University of Buenos Aires and other academic institutions.

The study said that in some districts the percentage of foreign owners already exceeds the current 15% cap.
