World.title: Prague to Restore Tram Service Between Holešovice and City Center
World.content:
Residents of Prague 7 will regain a tram connection between Holešovice and the city center from September, with tram line 5 set to operate through the district and continue toward Wenceslas Square.

The change follows months of pressure from Prague 7 officials and local residents, who have called for better tram connections since the cancellation of line 14.

The district had previously requested either the return of line 14 or the introduction of an equivalent service and organized a petition supporting the demand.



The new arrangement will initially be temporary. According to the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) system, two trams will operate on the route at least through December 2026.

Line 5 to replace temporary route

The new service is linked to planned transport changes in Žižkov. Because of a traffic closure there, tram line 34 will be replaced by line 5 in Holešovice.

At Holešovice train station, line 5 will connect with line 6, effectively creating a continuous service between the two routes. Trams will run from the station through the Holešovice area, past the market and across Vltavská Street before continuing toward Wenceslas Square and other parts of central Prague.

For passengers in Holešovice, the move restores a connection that was lost when line 14 was discontinued.

Service could change again next year

The situation between January and June 2027 has not yet been fully settled. According to PID, the final arrangement will depend in part on discussions between the incoming leaderships of Prague 3 and Prague 7.

Maintaining the additional tram service in Holešovice during that period could require limited reductions elsewhere in Prague 3. Another option would be to temporarily return to the existing arrangement using combined tram lines 6 and 34.

PID has warned that permanently combining lines 5 and 6 could also create delays at both ends of the route. Such a change could affect passengers travelling through Prague 2 and Prague 5, even though it would provide the direct connection sought by Prague 7.

World.title: “Ivan, Go Home!” Rally to Take Place Outside Russian Embassy in Prague
World.content:
A Czech-Ukrainian rally will take place outside the Russian Embassy in Prague on August 20 to mark the 58th anniversary of the Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The event, titled “Ivan, Go Home!”, is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. on Thursday, August 20, at Boris Němcova Square in Prague 6.

The rally comes one day before the anniversary of the night of August 20-21, 1968, when troops from five Warsaw Pact countries entered Czechoslovakia to crush the Prague Spring reform movement.



The invasion brought an end to the country’s attempt to pursue a more liberal form of socialism and was followed by two decades of political repression and Soviet military presence.

The event is being organized jointly by People in Need (Člověk v tísni), Memory of the People (Paměť národa), Million Moments for Democracy (Milion chvilek pro demokracii), and the European Congress of Ukrainians.

Organizers say the rally will connect the historical experience of the Soviet occupation with Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Participants will gather to remember those killed or persecuted following the 1968 invasion and the people who lived under the communist regime that followed. The organizers also plan to express support for Ukraine and draw attention to what they describe as the continuing use of imperial violence by Russia.

The choice of the rally’s name refers to one of the best-known slogans associated with the 1968 invasion. “Ivan, go home!” appeared on posters, walls, buildings and military vehicles as Czechoslovaks protested against the foreign troops occupying the country.

The invasion halted those reforms. Soviet troops remained in Czechoslovakia until the end of the communist era, while the subsequent period of “normalization” brought censorship, political purges and restrictions on civil liberties.

World.title: World of Warcraft Film Ibelin to Shoot in Prague
World.content:
Production of Ibelin, a new film based on the life of Norwegian World of Warcraft player Mats Steen, is moving to Prague this summer.

Filming is expected to take place at Barrandov Studios from early August through early October, following the production’s spring shoot in Norway.

The film is not connected to the 2016 Hollywood movie Warcraft. Instead, it tells the real-life story of Steen, who lived with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and built friendships, relationships and a social life inside the online world of World of Warcraft.



The Prague production is reportedly seeking extras for roles including blacksmiths, guards and innkeepers. The casting suggests that parts of the film set in the game’s fictional world could be filmed in the Czech Republic. The producers have not yet officially confirmed which scenes will be shot in Prague.

Charlie Plummer leads the cast

American actor Charlie Plummer will portray Mats Steen. Toni Collette and Stephen Graham will play his parents, while the supporting cast includes Bill Nighy, Isabela Merced, Maisy Stella, John Bradley and Ivanna Sakhno.

The film will be directed by Norwegian filmmaker Morten Tyldum, whose credits include The Imitation Game and the science-fiction film Passengers.

At the center of the story is the difference between Steen’s increasingly restricted physical existence and the freedom he experienced online. His character, known in World of Warcraft as Ibelin, became an important figure to people he met through the game.

One of Norway’s largest film projects

The Prague shoot is part of an international production with a reported budget of CZK 1 billion.

According to the Norwegian Film Institute, the project received 20 million Norwegian kroner in production support.

Ibelin is being produced by Vendôme Pictures, Pathé and Neby-Tyldum as an international co-production. The Norwegian Film Institute describes it as an English-language drama with a planned running time of around two hours.

The film is being developed for theatrical release, with its premiere currently expected in the third quarter of 2027.

World.title: GALLERY: Time Capsule Buried Beneath Prague’s Wenceslas Square Tramline
World.content:
A time capsule containing different items, newspapers and messages documenting life in 2026 has been buried beneath Prague’s reconstructed Wenceslas Square.

The capsule was placed on Wednesday, August 5, near the statue of St. Wenceslas as work continues on the upper section of the square.

The Prague New Town Association, which is involved in activities around the statue and the surrounding area, organised the ceremony.

The date was not originally chosen for its historical significance. Construction work ultimately determined both the day and the location of the burial. But the association later discovered that August 5 also marks the 60th anniversary of the release of the Beatles’ Revolver album.

“We were wondering what made August 5 go down in history. Then we found out that it was 60 years ago that the Beatles released their famous album Revolver. So now we are leaving a message here for future generations,” said Monika Vlková, the association’s executive director.



The box, measuring 60 by 40 by 23.5 centimetres and weighing about eight kilograms, was then taken to a prepared pit beside the statue. Workers had excavated the hole to a depth of around 1.7 metres, where the capsule was placed before the site was covered.

The container had been wrapped in transparent protective film, as had its contents.

The collection includes coins, newspapers published during the first week of August 2026, T-shirts, badges and written messages. It also contains proposals submitted by architects during the competition for the redesign of Wenceslas Square.

The box reportedly also holds a hammer and a beer glass.

The objects are accompanied by a 20-page report describing everyday life in the Czech capital in 2026. The capsule also contains USB drives with digital material documenting the period of the Covid-19 pandemic and its effects on life in central Prague.

The capsule is intended to remain underground for decades. The association estimates that Wenceslas Square could undergo another major reconstruction in roughly 50 years, although nobody can predict when the next intervention will actually take place.

World.title: Czechia Tightens Temporary Protection Rules for Ukrainian Men Aged 23 to 60
World.content:
New rules affecting Ukrainian men seeking temporary protection in the Czech Republic will take effect on August 5, 2026.

Under the changes, men aged 23 to 60 applying for temporary protection will have to demonstrate that they are exempt from military service in Ukraine.

The requirement will apply to new applications and certain other applications for protection, but not to people who already hold valid temporary protection.



The Czech Interior Ministry says the new rules follow an EU Council decision published in the Official Journal of the European Union on August 4. The decision also extends temporary protection for people fleeing Russia’s war in Ukraine until March 31, 2028.

For applicants aged 23 to 60, military registration documents will be checked as part of the application process. Applicants will use Ukraine’s Reserv+ system to demonstrate their military status, with the electronic military registration document showing whether they are exempt from military service.

The rules are different for younger applicants. People aged 18 to 22 will only need to demonstrate that they are registered in the Reserv+ system.

The new requirement concerns people applying for temporary protection for the first time, as well as repeat applications and applications connected with family reunification. It does not apply to people who already have valid temporary protection.

The military-service requirement will also not be introduced as part of the regular extension process. Ukrainians whose temporary protection is already valid will therefore not have to provide this additional documentation when extending their status through March 2028.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the Czech government had pushed for stricter conditions for new applicants. According to the ministry, the change is expected to reduce the number of new arrivals and ease pressure on public services, including health care and social security.

World.title: Filming of American Spy Series to Bring Restrictions to Prague 7
World.content:
Filming for the American series Birdwatcher will take place at the Prague 7 tax office on Kapitána Jaroše Embankment from August 8 to 24, bringing temporary restrictions to the area.

The production will use the tax office building at Kapitána Jaroše Embankment 1000/7, while part of the sidewalk outside the building will be closed to accommodate filming equipment.

The restrictions will not affect the normal operation of the tax office.



Drivers should also expect temporary parking restrictions on nearby Na Ovčinách Street. Vehicles will still be allowed to pass through the street, but parking will be prohibited during the designated filming periods.

The restrictions will not be in force continuously throughout the filming period. They will apply only on specific dates, with Prague 7 publishing a map showing the affected areas and individual dates on its website.

Prague has become a major filming location

Birdwatcher is an American spy fantasy series set during the Cold War. The production is being led by Legendary and Apple TV, with Andy Goddard directing. Wyatt Russell plays the lead role.

The story follows Colonel Lee Shaw as he embarks on a covert mission behind enemy lines to prevent the Soviet Union from unleashing a new Titan capable of devastating the United States and altering the balance of the Cold War.

The series is set in the 20th century against the backdrop of the Cold War, and parts of the production are being filmed in Prague.

Czech production company Stillking Films is handling the local production. The company has previously worked on major international productions filmed in the Czech capital, including The Gray Man.

World.title: Seven Prague Rooftops to Visit Before Summer Ends
World.content:
Summer is already moving on, and Prague’s rooftop season won’t last much longer.

August is the time to make the most of the city’s terraces, sunset views and outdoor events before they disappear for another year.

Here are seven rooftops and terraces worth visiting before autumn arrives.



1. REASON at Masaryčka

Eleven floors above Masaryk Station, REASON offers one of Prague’s newest rooftop dining spots, with views over the city and the Zaha Hadid-designed Masaryčka development.

This summer, its terrace is also home to the seasonal Frerejean Frères Champagne Bar, serving champagne by the glass, cocktails, oysters and light bites. The menu includes THE REASON KIR, made with herbs grown on the rooftop.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and cocktails above Masaryčka.

2. W Prague – ABOVE Rooftop

ABOVE Rooftop at W Prague brings a Mediterranean feel to the top of Wenceslas Square.

The daily Mediterranean Hour runs from 5 to 6 PM, with two spritzes and a Taste of the Mediterranean platter for CZK 990. Oysters are also served from Thursday to Saturday, alongside a programme of summer events and pop-ups.

This summer: Mediterranean Hour, sunset drinks and oysters in the centre.

3. MINUTY Rooftop Terrace

The rooftop at Fairmont Golden Prague offers views across Pařížská, Letná and the city centre from nine floors up.

MINUTY Rooftop Terrace by Golden Eye focuses on champagne, oysters, caviar and cocktails. The terrace is seasonal and is expected to remain open until September, weather permitting.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and caviar with a view.

4. Sky Lounge 360°

For the view alone, Sky Lounge 360° is hard to beat. The rooftop looks across Prague’s historic centre and becomes livelier during the summer months, with DJs, sunset events and Prague Rooftop Festival activities.

It is more about drinks and atmosphere than a long dinner — a good option for an evening that starts at sunset and continues after dark.

This summer: Sunset events, DJs and panoramic views.

5. The Cloud One Rooftop

The Cloud One Prague on Hybernská has its own rooftop cocktail bar overlooking the Masaryčka area.

The relaxed terrace works well for an after-work drink, while summer events bring DJs and a livelier atmosphere at sunset. It has also joined the Prague Rooftop Festival programme.

And if you want to make a night of it, REASON is just a short walk away.

This summer: Cocktails, sunset events and views of Masaryčka.

6. Casablanca Sky Bar

On the sixth floor of The President Hotel, Casablanca Sky Bar looks out over the Vltava and Prague skyline.

With DJs, cocktails and regular sunset events, it has more of a party atmosphere than a traditional hotel rooftop. It is also one of the venues taking part in the Prague Rooftop Festival.

This summer: DJs, cocktails and sunset parties above the Vltava.

7. Monkey Bar

Monkey Bar at Falkensteiner Hotel Prague is a quieter alternative, with a green, jungle-style terrace close to the main railway station.

Every Thursday until the end of August, the terrace hosts BBQ & Beats, combining barbecue, live music and summer drinks. Frozen margaritas are also on the menu.

For daytime plans, there is Jungle Brunch, including a bottomless mimosa option.

This summer: BBQ & Beats every Thursday through August.

World.title: Prague Kettlebell Brand Železná Koule Opens 600-Square-Metre Gym in Karlín
World.content:
Czech kettlebell training brand Železná koule has opened its largest location yet at Danube House in Prague’s Karlín district.

The new 600-square-metre gym expands the brand’s presence in Prague and comes ahead of the next edition of its flagship Amazing 12 fitness programme.

Železná koule has built a community around kettlebell training and coached workouts rather than the traditional self-service gym model. The company says more than 20,000 people have trained through its programmes since its launch.

At its Karlín location, members train under the guidance of coaches in small groups. The approach is designed to provide more personal instruction and a structured training environment, rather than simply giving members access to gym equipment.



The new location is also the latest venue for the company’s Amazing 12 programme, a 12-week fitness and body transformation course that combines regular training with nutrition guidance and ongoing support.

What is the Amazing 12 programme?

The programme is aimed at both people who are new to structured strength training and more experienced gym-goers looking for a more organised approach to their workouts.

Although the programme itself lasts 12 weeks, participants first complete a preparation week, making 13 weeks in total. During the programme, they take part in 64 training sessions, with one-hour workouts held every weekday under the supervision of a coach.

Groups are limited to a maximum of five participants, allowing coaches to work closely with each person throughout the programme.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Železná koule (@zelezna_koule)

The programme is designed to provide a structured routine covering exercise, nutrition and recovery, with progress tracked throughout the 12 weeks.

The next Amazing 12 programme starts on August 31, 2026, with places available at the new Karlín location as well as Železná koule gyms in Smíchov and Strašnice.

The Karlín opening is part of the continued expansion of a Czech fitness brand that has developed a following around kettlebell-based training and small-group coaching. For people unfamiliar with the name, Železná kloule roughly translates from Czech as “iron ball,” referring to the kettlebell at the centre of its training approach.

More information about the Amazing 12 programme, including registration, is available at amazing12.cz.

World.title: MÁV railway group preparing with extra services for the Sziget Festival – details
World.content:
The MÁV railway group will operate extra services for the Sziget Festival, the company told MTI on Friday.

During the festival, HEV suburban trains from Batthyany Square will run continuously with high capacity, meaning passengers can board six-carriage trains. The increased schedule will ensure access to and safe return from Obuda’s Hajogyari Island not only during the day but also at night, it added.

After concerts, trains will run every five minutes on average between 11pm and 1am on the Budapest section, while some additional services will operate only between Batthyány Square and Aquincum, with trains to Szentendre still running every 20 minutes.

The statement noted that a major concert attracting tens of thousands will take place on the island on Saturday evening, and the easiest way to get there is by H5 HEV or tram line 1. HEV services will be increased from 1pm, and from 4pm trains will run every five minutes towards Filatorigat. After a short walk from Filatorigát, the island can be reached via the K Bridge, it added.

If you missed: Will Hungary’s energy crisis derail Sziget Festival? Organisers reveal emergency power plan

Detailed timetables, transfer points, and ticket purchase options are available in the MAVPlusz app and on the MAV group’s official website (www.mavcsoport.hu/sziget), the statement said.

The number of visitors at Sziget Festival increased every year until 2017-2018, but after te COVID pancemic it has not yet been able to reach that peak again.

Photo: MTI

Sziget Festival 2026 wristband holders offered discounts across Budapest!

World.title: What could he have found? Georgian authorities send home Hungarian journalist who criticised Orbán-friendly government
World.content:
The Hungarian journalist who has reported extensively on the Georgian Dream government’s excesses – and its ever-closer ties to the Orbán administration and Moscow – has been effectively expelled from the Caucasian country. Local authorities cite irregularities in his residence permit; back home, newspapers suggest he may have stumbled upon something awkward in the nexus between the Orbán system and the Georgian ruling party, which is cultivating increasingly warm relations with Russia.

Detained, then sent home

László Róbert Mézes, a Hungarian journalist who has lived in the country for years and regularly filed reports for Magyar Hang on the country’s political crisis, anti-government protests and Georgian Dream’s grip on power, was taken into custody in Tbilisi before being deported. The Georgian Interior Ministry said Mézes was in the country “without legal grounds” and had exceeded the permitted period of stay, invoking a provision of the aliens’ law that allows detention where there is a risk of absconding. His lawyer maintained that his client’s stay was lawful. Mézes ultimately left the country at his own expense, escorted to the airport by migration officials.

Mézes leaves Georgia – at his own expense:

The case is notable not least because Mézes is no ordinary Hungarian correspondent based in Georgia: he has been an outspoken critic of Georgian Dream. For Magyar Hang, reporting from Tbilisi, he wrote repeatedly on the so-called “foreign agents” law – a near word‑for‑word translation of the Russian model – and on the suffocation of civil society and independent media, the blocking of voting rights for the diaspora (some one million of Georgia’s five million citizens, whose remittances underpin the economy), the imprisonment of opposition politicians and critical journalists, and the near‑constant street protests. He also reported for Magyar Hang that Prime Ministers Orbán and Fico were obstructing EU moves towards targeted sanctions against Georgian political leaders.

On the 612th day of protests following the 2024 election, he published these photographs last Saturday:

Beaten in Tbilisi – and he told Orbán what he thought

In October 2024, during Viktor Orbán’s visit to Tbilisi, Mézes shouted at the Hungarian Prime Minister in Hungarian that he had come to legitimise “stolen elections”, and asked whether he was proud that Georgian Dream was copying Fidesz. Orbán, alone among EU leaders, congratulated the victors almost immediately after the poll, while the rest of the EU (save Slovakia), the European Parliament, the Georgian President and the opposition all rejected the result. Mézes’s situation deteriorated further in September 2025: while working as a journalist at an anti-government demonstration, he was attacked by Georgian Dream activists outside the party headquarters. He was beaten, required stitches to his face and sustained hand injuries; Georgian authorities later formally recognised him as a victim.

In this post, featuring a photograph with Péter Magyar, he informed his Georgian followers that Péter Magyar would be the next Prime Minister:

A pro‑Russian turn

Although the Caucasian country was at war with Russia in 2008 over South Ossetia and Abkhazia – territories occupied by Moscow and subsequently recognised as independent states – the Georgian Dream party has lately been cultivating conspicuously pragmatic relations with Putin’s Russia. The “foreign agents” law, passed in 2024 on the Russian model, targeted critical NGOs and media outlets; in November 2024 the government announced it would not commence EU accession talks until 2028. Tbilisi has not joined sanctions against Russia and continues to trade with Moscow, even though diplomatic relations have never been restored since the 2008 war.

If you missed: Georgian-Israeli businessman linked to former propaganda minister Rogán allegedly sought to gain access to key aide of PM Péter Magyar

Good relations to be maintained, PM Péter Magyar pledges

Péter Magyar, Hungary’s prime minister-elect, said at a press conference shortly after the 12 April election that he would maintain good relations with Georgia. Asked by a reporter from the pro-government Georgian broadcaster Rustavi 2, Magyar said that the fact Viktor Orbán’s government had forged strong ties with a country in the Balkans – or anywhere else – did not mean Hungary would have a less close relationship with that country.

“But if Hungary has bad relations with a country, we will improve them, because it is in our shared interest to work together, to co-operate and to prosper together,” he added, according to civil.ge. Magyar also said he was open to visiting Tbilisi and looked forward to working with the Georgian government.

“But we are not going to interfere in the internal affairs of other countries. We will not try to influence elections in your country, North Macedonia or anywhere else. That’s not our style, and it is not the job of any European government. Everyone is elected to support and represent the electorate of their own country,” he said.

The media outlet noted that Irakli Kobakhidze, Georgia’s prime minister, had visited Hungary on 21 March to address CPAC Budapest and express his support for Mr Orbán. On 13 April, following the Tisza party’s victory in Hungary’s general election, the Georgian Government congratulated Mr Magyar and his party, while thanking Orbán for his “outstanding and steadfast support for Georgia’s national interests and the Georgian people over the years”.

Hungary sent fake observers to Georgia’s elections

World.title: PM Magyar shared good news about voluntary consumption cuts as heat records were broken again
World.content:
There will be no need for voluntary consumption cuts from Friday, PM Péter Magyar announced on his Facebook page on Thursday evening.

Magyar said: “Together, we did it, and we protected our country’s energy security. Thank you, Hungary!” He added that the Defence Council’s decisions will be announced on Friday morning.

Multiple heat records, along with a wind-speed record, were broken on Thursday, the weather service HungaroMet said on Facebook, citing preliminary data. The new national daytime heat record was recorded in Kiskunfélegyháza, where the temperature reached 41.8 degrees Celsius, surpassing the previous record of 40.2 C set in Orosháza in 1905.

Danube water crisis: hotel ships and cargo vessels stranded in Hungary

Budapest also saw a new daytime and all-time heat record of 41.6 C, recorded at the Ujpest station. The previous daily record for the capital was 37.8 C in 2012 at the Budapest city centre station, while the previous absolute record was set on Wednesday at the Újpest station.

Meanwhile, a thunderstorm also led to a new daily wind-speed record in Szolnok, where a gust of 113kmh was recorded. The previous daily wind record was 107kmh in Körösladány in 2010.

Amid water and energy crisis, Hungary is to elect new president within days – PM Magyar’s Tisza to decide this week

World.title: PM Magyar: Orbán knew that Hungary’s energy system was on the brink of collapse, but failed to act
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar on Thursday accused the former prime minister, Viktor Orbán, of knowing that Hungary’s energy system was on the brink of collapse but failing to act.

Hungary could not provide as much electricity as Orbán promised

In a video posted on Facebook, Magyar quoted a 2022 bill submitted by the previous government, which stated that Hungary’s energy supply was on the edge of a precipice because the government had burdened the system with a “full Paks-worth” of electricity demand to benefit major investors, MTI wrote.

“In other words, they promised more electricity to major industrial players, often battery investment projects, than the domestic energy system could safely provide,” the prime minister said. Magyar said Hungary needed “an energy and water revolution”, including “unprecedented development” of energy storage capacities and the electricity grid.

Negative prices for solar energy

Magyar noted that while Hungary has over 8,800MW of solar capacity, its energy storage capacity is only 980MW, meaning the country can produce roughly nine times more energy from the sun than its storage facilities can absorb at any given moment. As a result, Hungary often produces surplus energy during sunny periods, which it can only sell at minimal or even negative prices, yet it struggles to store enough for night-time or cloudier conditions, he explained.

Despite this, he said, the Orbán government had consistently removed requirements for storage capacity development from regulations and subsidy programmes for industrial and residential solar projects. He vowed that the current government would develop energy storage capacity to reduce Hungary’s import dependence.

Magyar also blamed the previous government for the underdevelopment of the electricity grid. He said that on Friday, the government will announce the results of a nearly 600 billion forint (EUR 1.7bn) EU-funded tender to develop the electricity grid, enabling the construction of new power lines, substations and higher-capacity transformers. “Hungary’s energy will be safer, cheaper and increasingly domestic,” he said.

If you missed – Danube water crisis: hotel ships and cargo vessels stranded in Hungary

Water and energy crises almost over

Referring to the current heatwave and drought, which has led to a reduction in output of the Paks plant, the prime minister noted that major industrial consumers are still expected to voluntarily reduce energy consumption, and he thanked the public for avoiding or rescheduling electricity use between 5pm and 10pm.

Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

Magyar added that the Danube’s water level at Paks has risen by 11cm since Sunday, and rain is currently falling in the Austrian catchment areas. However, this will likely not be enough to fully restore Hungary’s nuclear power plant, and a new period of dry, hot weather is expected next week, meaning “we will have to count every centimetre again,” he said.

World.title: Budapest city centre roads to be closed this morning after explosives found in the Danube
World.content:
Szabadság Bridge and the Buda embankments near the Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) will be temporarily closed early Friday morning due to the removal of explosive devices from the Danube, the Hungarian Armed Forces’ bomb disposal unit said on Thursday.

Last weekend, the unit received two reports of unexploded devices found near the Danube’s Raoul Wallenberg embankment and near the Valdemar and Nina Langlet embankment.

On Tuesday, a bomb disposal patrol identified the devices near the Raoul Wallenberg embankment as a Soviet-era 203mm concrete-piercing shell from the Second World War and a suspected 19th-century cannonball. Near BME, they identified a German Second World War-era supply container holding eight Panzerfaust launch tubes, their warheads and detonators.

Budapest, Szabadság Bridge. Source: John Woods/DNH

At 4 AM on Friday, Szabadság Bridge and the entire length of the Raoul Wallenberg embankment will be closed to remove the devices.

World.title: Danube water crisis: hotel ships and cargo vessels stranded in Hungary
World.content:
Eleven river cruise ships are currently waiting on the Hungarian stretch of the Danube because of exceptionally low water levels, while most cargo vessels have also been forced to halt operations, Hungary’s Ministry of Transport and Investment (KBM) told the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) on Wednesday.

10 cm needed between riverbed and hull

The ministry said low water levels were currently hampering the movement of deeper-draught vessels not only in Hungary but along the entire 2,412-kilometre navigable stretch of the river. For safety reasons, vessels must maintain a clearance of at least 10 centimetres between their hulls and the riverbed.

As a result, some cargo vessels can operate only after drastically reducing their loads, in some cases to just 10 to 20 per cent of their normal carrying capacity, the ministry said.

The authorities stressed that water-management agencies regularly survey the river, while the navigation authority issues official notices warning vessels about shoals where the standard navigable depth of 270 centimetres is no longer available.

A German cargo ship in Budapest. Photo: Creative Commons CC BY-SA 3.0

Several stretches of the Hungarian Danube too shallow

The water level determines the maximum draught that can safely be accommodated on each section of the river. At the current levels, several stretches of the Hungarian Danube have become too shallow for normal commercial navigation.

If you missed: Did the Danube run dry in Budapest and Paks because the Slovaks diverted it?

The navigation authority is not imposing a blanket restriction on shipping because of the low water levels. Instead, the master of each vessel is responsible for deciding whether it is safe to proceed, taking into account the latest published water levels and information on shoals, as well as the vessel’s own draught, the ministry said.

The number of stranded river cruise ships has nevertheless fallen in recent days. According to an earlier statement from the ministry, 15 cruise ships were still waiting on the Hungarian section of the Danube last Tuesday.

World.title: Hungary’s political divide is shocking: even during a water and energy crisis, we are still blaming one another
World.content:
The energy crisis caused by extreme heat and drought has prompted a substantial proportion of Hungarians to change their daily habits: cutting electricity and water consumption now affects a majority of the adult population. Yet the political fault lines are more apparent than anywhere else when it comes to managing the crisis, while attitudes towards recovery reveal a more generational divide, according to new research by Europion. There is, however, one thing on which Hungarians are broadly united.

Most Hungarians understand that the situation is serious

The survey asked respondents who completed the questionnaire via an app who or what was responsible for the current situation, and how it should be tackled. One unequivocally positive finding was that 85 per cent of Hungarians aged 16 and over had reduced their electricity use to some degree, while 78 per cent had also cut back on water consumption.

Europion

For almost one in eight people, however, saving electricity had not involved any change at all: 12 per cent said they had done nothing to reduce their energy use. In the past, certain Fidesz-linked websites and influencers eagerly urged people to run their air conditioning at full blast all day and fill their swimming pools in order to worsen the difficulties faced by the Tisza government. The survey did not examine whether there was any connection between the two.

The most common change was using household appliances less frequently, cited by half of respondents. Many were also saving water when irrigating their gardens, washing their cars and using air conditioning. These measures were mentioned by 46 per cent, 45 per cent and 40 per cent of respondents respectively.

Political camps emerge everywhere

At first sight, public opinion of the government’s handling of the crisis appears more favourable: half of respondents gave it a good or excellent rating, while 26 per cent rated its performance a fail or a bare pass. Political allegiance, however, had a remarkably strong influence on people’s views.

Some 81 per cent of Tisza voters rated the government’s performance positively, compared with just 13 per cent of Fidesz supporters. Critical voices were also in the majority among Mi Hazánk voters, while those who did not vote in April’s election and supporters of other parties tended to take a more favourable view of the government’s measures.

Europion

Similar divisions emerged over who should be blamed for the situation. The largest group, 40 per cent, pointed to the failings of the previous government; 34 per cent blamed extreme weather and climate change, while 18 per cent cited the current government’s lack of preparedness.

Political affiliation once again distorted these figures sharply. Some 68 per cent of Tisza voters blamed the Orbán governments, which had been in power for 16 years. Among Fidesz supporters, by contrast, 45 per cent highlighted the unpreparedness of the current cabinet, which had been in office for barely three months.

Europion

Hungarians favour voluntary restrictions

There is considerably more agreement over whether compulsory restrictions are necessary. Some 51 per cent of respondents said measures based on voluntary reductions in consumption would be sufficient, while only 27 per cent would support tougher rules or sanctions.

Political camps were also closer together on this issue. Support for stricter measures ranged from 23 to 30 per cent across the various groups, while backing for voluntary solutions stood at between 42 and 59 per cent.

Europion

If you missed: Did the Danube run dry in Budapest and Paks because the Slovaks diverted it?

How can Hungary emerge from the crisis? A generational divide

When it comes to the country’s future energy mix, the balance tilts towards renewables. Just 9 per cent would rely primarily on nuclear power, while 42 per cent would favour renewables and a further 42 per cent would use the two energy sources in equal measure.

Support for renewables was stronger among younger people, while nuclear power attracted a larger share of Fidesz voters and older respondents.

Europion questioned 1,600 people through its panel of mobile and web applications on August 4. The researchers adjusted the data using the MRP method to account for sampling distortions; the maximum margin of error for the estimates was 2.5 percentage points.

World.title: Is shopping abroad really cheaper? Why are Romanians and Bulgarians outspending Hungarians? New study provides answers
World.content:
A new study suggests that Hungarians are right to feel that shopping abroad can be cheaper – but much depends on what they are buying. Food prices paint a very different picture from, say, the cost of services. Meanwhile, a fresh survey has shown that Romania and Bulgaria still outperform Hungary on an important measure of consumption. A new analysis now attempts to set the record straight.

Is shopping abroad cheaper? Yes – but it depends what you buy

Many Hungarians will be familiar with the experience of travelling abroad and finding that certain products cost the same as, or even less than, they do at home. At the same time, wages remain well below Western European levels. A recent analysis by GKI Economic Research examined how much Hungary has actually moved closer to the European Union over the past 15 years, both in terms of wages and prices.

The figures show progress on both fronts, but Hungary did not start from the same base in each case. In 2010, Hungary’s price level stood at 59 per cent of the EU average, while wages reached just 32 per cent of the bloc-wide average. By 2025, the price level had risen to 72 per cent of the EU average, while wages had reached 49 per cent.

Photo: Daily News Hungary

In other words, Hungarian wages have moved closer to the EU average faster than prices have. In theory, that should mean an improvement in purchasing power. According to GKI, however, there is an important downside: many of Hungary’s regional competitors – including Romania, Poland and Slovakia – have developed considerably faster.

Food is already almost at EU prices

Hungarian consumers may be particularly interested in the significant differences that have emerged between individual product groups. In 2025, food prices had already reached 95 per cent of the EU average. This means that Hungarians are buying fruit, vegetables and dairy products at prices that are almost at the EU level. Alcohol and tobacco products were cheaper, at 87 per cent of the EU average, while furniture and household appliances stood at 89 per cent.

Shopping abroad: an Auchan store in Târgu Mureș, Romania. Photo: depositphotos.com

Housing and household utilities might initially appear to be an exception, with prices standing at 67 per cent of the EU average. GKI said, however, that this figure is significantly distorted by the impact of Hungary’s household utility price cuts and other forms of state support. The costs associated with housing have risen substantially in recent years.

Meanwhile, the cost of services has also edged closer to EU levels. Between 2010 and 2025, prices in tourism moved 33 percentage points closer to the EU average, education by 31 percentage points, and leisure and culture by 14 percentage points.

Wages remain well below the EU average

The most important gap, however, remains visible in wages. Although Hungarian earnings have improved significantly relative to the EU average since 2010, they still stood at only 49 per cent of it in 2025.

GKI also stressed that it matters how Hungary has performed compared with its own starting point. Several neighbouring countries have caught up at a much faster pace, meaning that Hungary has failed to improve its relative position despite making progress of its own.

If you missed: Czech business paper explains how and why Tesco will withdraw from Hungary

Hungary ranks last on this measure of consumption

This is reflected in figures for actual individual consumption per head, on which Hungary ranks last in the EU. In other words, although Hungarians earn more in nominal terms today, and wages have moved closer to the EU average, the spending power of the average Hungarian household remains the weakest in the bloc – even below that of average households in Romania and Bulgaria.

GKI therefore rejects the idea that Hungary has made no progress in catching up with Europe. Wages have indeed risen faster relative to the EU average than prices have. The problem is that Hungary’s rate of convergence has lagged behind that of its regional competitors, while the prices of certain goods and services are already close to EU levels.

Hungarians travelling abroad may therefore reasonably encounter prices – particularly for food – that no longer appear higher than those at home. When it comes to wages, however, the gap remains substantial.

World.title: Thriller starring Nicolas Cage to open this year's horror and fantastic film fest in Biertan
World.content:
The Full Moon Horror and Fantastic Film Festival, presented by the Transilvania International Film Festival, returns to Biertan for its 11th edition, bringing three days and three nights of premieres, cult films and open-air screenings.

The festival opens with the Romanian premiere of The Carpenter’s Son, starring Nicolas Cage. Another highlight of this year’s edition will be the cine-concert Trenul Fantomă, featuring live music by Dubase, preceded by an acoustic performance by Ana Coman and her guitar as part of Full Moon Unplugged.

At Bastion Open Air, the programme kicks off on Friday, August 14, with Nightborn, the new film by Finnish director Hanna Bergholm, known to horror audiences for Hatching. Selected for the competition at the Berlin International Film Festival, the film follows a couple who move into an isolated house in the Finnish woods, where the arrival of their first child awakens a disturbing presence. The evening continues with The Rocky Horror Picture Show, the horror musical that has become one of cinema’s great cult phenomena. The story behind the film will also be explored from behind the scenes in the documentary Strange Journey: The Story of Rocky Horror, screening on Saturday at Cinema Ion Hobana.

On Saturday, Bastion Open Air will screen Her Private Hell, the new film by director Nicolas Winding Refn, as well as the original Dutch version of the thriller The Vanishing. The programme also includes the 1993 American remake, also directed by George Sluizer, giving audiences an opportunity to compare the two versions.

On Sunday, Carrie returns to the Bastion screen. Directed by Brian De Palma and based on Stephen King’s novel, the classic marks 50 years since its release.

On Friday, August 14, Méliès Open Air will host the Romanian premiere of The Carpenter’s Son. Directed by Lotfy Nathan, the supernatural thriller stars Nicolas Cage as Joseph, alongside FKA twigs as Mary and Noah Jupe as their teenage son.

On Saturday, August 15, audiences are invited to the cine-concert Trenul Fantomă. Made in 1933 by Jean Mihail, the first Romanian-language talking film tells the story of travelers forced to spend the night at a railway station believed to be haunted. The film will be screened with live music performed by Dubase.

The Méliès programme concludes on Sunday, August 16, with The Virgin of the Quarry Lake, directed by Laura Casabé. Inspired by the prose of writer Mariana Enríquez, the film blends adolescence, jealousy and black magic against the backdrop of Argentina’s 2001 crisis.

The selection continues at Cinema Karloff and Cinema Ion Hobana, with titles including The Turkish Coffee Table, Gaua, Species, Roqia, Veins, The Uncertainty Principle, Feels Like Home, Anemoneciacs and Transylvania Tapes.

The program also includes Romanian short films, the documentary Strange Journey: The Story of Rocky Horror, and repeat screenings of The Carpenter’s Son, Nightborn and Her Private Hell.

The festival takes place between August 14 and August 16.

World.title: Romania’s Banca Transilvania extends EUR 71.4 mln loan for Entek Elektrik PV park
World.content:
The largest bank in Romania, Banca Transilvania, announced that it will finance the development of the Eco Sun Niculești photovoltaic park, Entek Elektrik’s first investment in local green energy production, with EUR 71.4 million.

It is one of the largest bilateral financings granted to a photovoltaic project under development in the country. Once completed, the park, located in Dâmbovița County, will have an installed capacity of approximately 205 MW. The total value of the project is estimated at EUR 100 million.

“Projects of this scale contribute to strengthening energy independence and modernizing the Romanian economy. We are pleased to support Entek Elektrik’s first investment in renewable energy production in Romania and to continue the solid partnership that we have built together,” said Cosmin Călin, Deputy General Manager Large Corporate, Banca Transilvania.

The investment in the Eco Sun Niculești project is made through Entek Elektrik Üretimi A.Ş., the renewable energy company of the Koç Group, and its main shareholder is Türkiye Petrol Refinerileri A.Ş. (Tüpraş), the largest industrial company in Turkey and the seventh largest refinery operator in Europe.

In Turkey, Entek owns an energy capacity portfolio of 550 MW. The company aims to further expand its renewable energy portfolio and seeks to become one of the leading green energy producers in Turkey.

World.title: Survey: Healthcare services, energy, utilities & recycling emerge as top PE investment picks in Romania
World.content:
In Romania, the sector of healthcare services is expected to attract the highest level of investor interest in 2026, followed by energy, utilities & recycling, a sector that has climbed sharply in private equity funds’ rankings of preferred investment areas, the Roland Berger European Private Equity Outlook 2026 shows.

These preferences reflect local funds’ focus on resilient sectors with strong fundamentals and a greater ability to withstand a volatile economic environment, according to the survey.

The local investors’ interest in the IT sector is more moderate in 2026 compared with previous years. The sector of consumer goods and retail, which previously ranked among private equity funds’ preferred ones, is also continuing to lose some of its appeal amid macroeconomic uncertainty and pressure on consumer spending.

By contrast, investors in Western Europe and other Central and Eastern European countries continue to favor sectors such as technology, logistics and B2B services, and infrastructure, where structural growth trends and scaling opportunities remain key factors driving private equity funds’ interest.

At the same time, funds in more mature markets are continuing to specialize by sector. The majority of respondents in Western Europe expect to further concentrate their investments in specific industries this year, reflecting the increasing complexity of sectors and the growing need for specialized expertise to assess and develop portfolio companies.

Despite a significant deterioration in the macroeconomic environment compared with previous years and increased political uncertainty, private equity funds active in Romania continue to show an appetite for new investments, the report shows.

The industry is entering a new phase, in which competitive advantage is gradually shifting from access to capital towards execution capabilities and value creation, according to the report.

“Approximately 80% of respondents in Romania expect an economic slowdown in 2026, marking a significant shift from the optimism expressed in previous editions of the study. Nevertheless, investment appetite remains solid. Half of the funds based in Romania expect the number of private equity transactions carried out locally to increase in 2026 compared with the previous year, despite 2025 already being a very dynamic year with a high number of transactions,” Szabolcs Nemes, managing partner at Roland Berger Romania, explained.

“Investors see political instability, the challenging macroeconomic environment and increasingly intense competition for attractive companies as the main challenges for the period ahead. In this context, funds that can generate proprietary deal opportunities while maintaining investment discipline will have a significant competitive advantage,” he added.

Szabolcs Nemes, managing partner at Roland Berger Romania

According to the study, around 60% of funds active in Romania intend to expand their regional footprint in the period ahead by entering one or two new markets. They are targeting both direct investments and add-on acquisitions, with neighboring countries such as Bulgaria and Moldova among their priorities, as well as larger markets in the region such as Poland. The main objective of this regional expansion is to create regional champions by capitalizing on consolidation and scaling opportunities available across many sectors of the economy. Investors identify cultural integration, management team capabilities, and a lack of local expertise as the main challenges related to expansion, the study found.

Alina Florean, Senior Manager at Roland Berger Romania

“Given the relatively small size of local markets, regional expansion is no longer simply a growth opportunity but has become a strategic necessity for many funds in the region. However, levels of maturity vary, and the strategies adopted differ significantly,” Alina Florean, Senior Manager at Roland Berger Romania, said.

“Funds originating in Poland and the Czech Republic are already active across the region and are therefore primarily focused on consolidating their existing platforms. By contrast, many funds originating in Romania and Southeast Europe, including Bulgaria and Croatia, are only now taking their first steps towards international expansion,” she added.

The Romania & CEE Focus Report complements the 2026 edition of the Roland Berger European Private Equity Outlook. Around 3,500 industry professionals across Europe were invited to participate in this year's edition. In Romania, more than 80% of active funds participated, while the participation rate in the rest of the CEE region exceeded 50%.

World.title: Romanian citizen arrested for espionage in Germany
World.content:
A Romanian citizen accused of espionage has been arrested in Germany, based on a warrant issued by the Federal Court of Justice in Rheine, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

“The German authorities have executed an arrest warrant issued by the Federal Court of Justice in Rheine (North Rhine-Westphalia), under which a Romanian citizen was arrested. We mention that, up to this moment, no requests for consular assistance have been registered at the level of the Consulate General of Romania in Bonn from the Romanian citizen concerned or from his family,” MAE specified in a press release.

The arrest is allegedly connected to a Russian-sponsored assassination attempt.

Earlier this week, Die Zeit announced that Russian secret services allegedly planned to assassinate Stefan Thumann, director of the German drone manufacturer Donaustahl. The attack was prevented thanks to the rapid reaction of the German security services, which had received a warning from the intelligence agencies of partner countries.

The publication reported that in the spring of this year, German police arrested two suspects in Spain and in North Rhine-Westphalia: a Ukrainian man, Serhii N., and a Romanian woman, Alla S. According to investigators, between December 2025 and March 2026, they surveilled Thumann near his residence, photographing and filming his home and the company headquarters. They also gathered information about him from open sources.

In December 2025, German intelligence services received information from a foreign partner agency indicating that Thumann was probably in danger. Shortly afterwards, Bavarian officers detained Serhii N., confiscated his mobile phones and copied large volumes of data. However, because of time constraints, they were unable to fully analyze the devices while he was in custody, and he was released.

Subsequent analyses indicated that he had probably been in contact with Russian intelligence services. Investigators also discovered possible attempts to spy on Thumann’s father in Starnberg, Bavaria, in order to find out where his son was located.

By then, however, Serhii N. had fled to Spain together with his family. Meanwhile, Alla S. continued to surveil Thumann in Germany.

World.title: Romania’s High Court clears trial of far-right ex-candidate Georgescu and mercenary leader Potra
World.content:
Romania’s High Court of Cassation and Justice decided on Thursday, 6 August, that the trial in which far-right former presidential candidate Călin Georgescu and mercenary leader Horațiu Potra, along with 20 other defendants, were accused of actions against the constitutional order may begin.

As part of the ruling, the Court rejected the appeals filed both by the Public Ministry and by the defendants in the preliminary chamber procedure. Instead, it upheld the April 2 decision of the Bucharest Court of Appeal, allowing the trial to start, according to Libertatea.

During the procedure, the case was resumed after a change in the composition of the judicial panel, and the ruling was postponed several times.

Georgescu is accused of complicity in the attempt to commit acts against the constitutional order and of communicating false information in a continuing manner. Potra, in turn, is accused of attempting to commit actions against the constitutional order, non-compliance with the weapons and ammunition regime, and non-compliance with the explosives regime. His son and nephew, Dorian Potra and Alexandru Potra, were also sent to trial for attempting to commit actions against the constitutional order.

Prosecutors claim that after the decision of the Constitutional Court of December 6, 2024, to annul the presidential elections, Călin Georgescu and Horațiu Potra met at an equestrian complex in Ciolpani, Ilfov County. During that meeting, a plan was allegedly discussed through which persons with military training from Horațiu Potra’s entourage were to carry out violent actions aimed at diverting public demonstrations.

Afterwards, according to prosecutors, Horațiu Potra allegedly organized a paramilitary group made up of 21 people, which was supposed to travel to Bucharest to participate in protests that would allegedly be transformed into violent actions. Before they could arrive, however, they were stopped by police on the night of December 7 to 8. Following the checks, bladed weapons, pistols, pepper sprays, telescopic batons, pyrotechnic materials and other objects considered dangerous were discovered.

Prosecutors claim that the defendants’ actions created a state of danger for the constitutional order and national security.

Călin Georgescu has also been sent to trial in a second case, in which he is accused of Legionary propaganda and the public promotion of persons convicted of genocide and war crimes.

With regards Horațiu Potra, the High Court decided in June 2026 to replace preventive detention with house arrest. His son and nephew had previously been placed under judicial control.

World.title: Romania’s PNL and USR challenge Integrity Law before Constitutional Court
World.content:
Romania's National Liberal Party (PNL) and Save Romania Union (USR) have referred the recently adopted Integrity Law to the Constitutional Court (CCR), arguing that one of its key provisions violates the constitutional principle prohibiting the retroactive application of legislation, Ziarul Financiar reported.

The law is a milestone under Romania's National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR). If it is not enacted by August 31, Romania risks losing a EUR 771 million grant under the European Union's Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF).

The constitutional challenge focuses on an amendment adopted by Parliament at the initiative of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), which provides that local elected officials previously found to have been in a conflict of interest would lose their mandates once the new law enters into force, even though the legislation in force at the time did not impose such a sanction.

PNL and USR argue that the provision breaches Article 15 of Romania's Constitution, which stipulates that laws apply only to future situations, except where new criminal provisions are more favourable to the accused.

The amendment has been widely linked to the case of Timișoara Mayor Dominic Fritz. Romania's National Integrity Agency (ANI), with the finding subsequently upheld by the courts, determined that Fritz had been in a conflict of interest after approving an urban planning document involving a local councillor who had previously lent him money during an electoral campaign.

Following the constitutional challenge, PSD accused PNL and USR on August 6 of jeopardising the EUR 771 million RRF grant by delaying the law's entry into force.

The Social Democrats argued that referring the legislation to the Constitutional Court risks preventing Romania from meeting the August 31 deadline attached to the reform milestone. However, the party did not address the opposition's argument that the contested amendment may be unconstitutional because it applies sanctions retroactively.

The Constitutional Court will now determine whether the disputed provisions comply with the Constitution. Its ruling will also determine whether the legislation can be promulgated in time for Romania to fulfil the relevant RRF commitment.

World.title: Romania’s Transgaz explores investment in US LNG export project
World.content:
Romania's state-controlled gas transmission operator Transgaz signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with US-based Argent LNG on August 6 to explore a potential strategic equity investment in the developer of a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminal in Port Fourchon, Louisiana, according to Bursa.

Argent LNG is developing an export terminal at Port Fourchon with a planned capacity of 25 million metric tonnes per year (Mtpa). The project is expected to deliver its first commercial cargo in 2030.

The non-binding agreement, signed at Transgaz's headquarters in Bucharest, establishes a framework for negotiations on a possible Transgaz stake in Argent LNG alongside other US investors.

According to the companies, the initiative would allow Transgaz to strengthen its long-term access to US LNG supplies while participating directly in the development of one of North America's largest planned LNG export facilities.

Beyond securing LNG supplies, the memorandum envisages using Romania's gas transmission network as a regional transit corridor for US LNG destined for the Republic of Moldova, Ukraine and other Central and Eastern European countries, including Hungary, Austria, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Germany.

The agreement does not commit either party to an investment, with any potential participation by Transgaz remaining subject to further negotiations and the completion of the necessary commercial and regulatory procedures.

World.title: EC argues against Romania’s plans to defer closure of coal power plants
World.content:
The European Commission (EC) argues that Romania has not demonstrated that meeting the decarbonisation targets would put its power security at risk and furthermore warns that the targets set under the Resilience Facility can no longer be revised due to the short time left until the scheme expires, according to Profit.ro.

Romania’s power grid operator contracted a study that it argues justifies deferring the shutdown of several coal-fired power plants behind the targets set under milestone 119a, part of the fix (and final) disbursement request under RRF with a EUR 771 million grant attached.

The Decarbonisation Law as recently approved by Parliament, subject to promulgation, reportedly breaches the requirements set in milestone 119a and will result in losing the attached grant, the Minister of Investments and European Projects, Dragos Pîslaru, said.

Furthermore, Pîslaru invoked, in Parliament, a technical letter from the European Commission confirming that, following such a law, Romania will no longer be able to submit payment requests for PNRR funds and will face penalties, with the other decarbonization milestone, 114, also being affected in a retroactive manner.

The EC interprets the official opinion of the European Union Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER) on the adequacy study prepared by Transelectrica to mean that the study did not demonstrate that the closure of Romanian coal-fired power plants within the deadlines assumed by the PNRR and decarbonization legislation would endanger Romania's security of energy supply.

Under a different interpretation, Transelectrica recommends "maintaining in operation three lignite-fired units at Rovinari, of which one is in technical reserve, and two units at Turceni, of which one is in technical reserve.

Brussels' position is based on the fact that ACER identified unjustified methodological deviations in the adequacy study, which may lead to the wrong estimation of security of supply parameters, with a significant impact on the results of the study.

However, beyond the adequacy study, the Commission considers that it is no longer possible to renegotiate the PNRR regarding decarbonization milestone 119a, as there is no more time for this, given that the milestone remained unchanged at the July 2026 review, and the implementation of the PNRR ends on August 31, 2026.
